A unified decision model for Bayesian ambiguity and non-affine statistics

Zachary Van Oosten ††thanks: Department of Decision Sciences, HEC Montréal, Canada. zachary.van-oosten@hec.ca    Ruodu Wang ††thanks: Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science, University of Waterloo, Canada. wang@uwaterloo.ca
October 15, 2026
Abstract

This paper studies decision functionals under ambiguity when pure-risk evaluation is determined by a general, possibly non-affine statistic. We represent ambiguity perception by a Bayesian second-order model over first-order models and encode ambiguity attitude with a separate parameter. We formulate four consistency and monotonicity properties for decision functionals combining these objects. We show that second-order averaging does not generally preserve these properties for non-affine statistics, including expected shortfall, the industry-standard risk measure. To address this limitation, we introduce an ambiguity iron, a mapping from a second-order model and an ambiguity attitude to an ambiguity set of first-order models. Worst-case evaluation over this set preserves the chosen statistic as the pure-risk criterion. We construct an ambiguity iron by distorting the second-order model and show that it produces convex and compact sets of predictive models. We derive formulas for several classes of statistics and, in parametric settings, a sample-based approximation for the distorted expectation. Portfolio examples illustrate how ambiguity perception and attitude affect evaluations and allocations. Under posterior concentration and continuity of the parametrization, the ambiguity sets contract, and the associated decision functionals converge to their pure-risk values. We also describe a KL-based robustification for possible model misspecification.

Keywords: Knightian uncertainty, model uncertainty, expected shortfall, model misspecification

 

1 Introduction

Decision functionals assign numerical values to choice objects under uncertainty. In this paper, choice objects are real-valued acts. We begin with a simple construction of decision models, where the decision maker’s preferences depend on two ingredients: a statistic that represents how the DM evaluates distributions and a first-order model that specifies the probability description of future states. An act is evaluated by applying the statistic to its distribution under the first-order model. This construction separates an act’s probabilistic description from its evaluation and appears, for example, in portfolio selection (Markowitz, 1952), statistical decision theory (Savage, 1954), and financial risk management (Artzner et al., 1999).

This construction presumes that the decision maker (DM) can identify a unique first-order model. Following Knight (1921), we distinguish between pure risk, where this model is known, and ambiguity, where it cannot be uniquely identified. The distinction is reflected in the behavior described by Ellsberg (1961). Under ambiguity, a decision functional should incorporate both the perception of ambiguity and the DM’s reaction to it. These components need not coincide: the same perception of ambiguity may combine with different ambiguity attitudes, while the same attitude may apply to different perceptions.

Two common approaches emphasize different parts of this problem. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) represents ambiguity by a set of first-order models, called an ambiguity set, and evaluates an act by its worst-case value over that set. Rooted in the maxmin expected utility model of Gilboa and Schmeidler (1989), this approach is used in portfolio selection (El Ghaoui et al., 2003; Natarajan et al., 2008; Zhu and Fukushima, 2009), risk measurement (Delage et al., 2019; Fadina et al., 2024; Mao et al., 2026), robust optimization (Delage and Ye, 2010; Ben-Tal et al., 2013), and actuarial science (Blanchet et al., 2019; Birghila and Pflug, 2019). It allows the same ambiguity set to be combined with different statistics. The set must nevertheless be specified, and the construction alone does not determine how it changes with new information. A Bayesian approach instead represents uncertainty about the first-order model with a second-order model: a probability measure over first-order models. Bayesian updating then provides a learning mechanism. An ambiguity-neutral benchmark averages the second-order model to obtain the predictive first-order model and evaluates acts under that model. This benchmark is used in financial risk management (Ardia, 2008; Ardia et al., 2017), actuarial science (Klugman, 1992; Cairns, 2000), and portfolio allocation (Kandel and Stambaugh, 1996; Feng and He, 2022). However, it does not encode attitudes toward ambiguity.

The smooth ambiguity model of Klibanoff et al. (2005) combines second-order beliefs with ambiguity-sensitive evaluation. In its expected-loss formulation, the inner loss function represents pure-risk preferences, the second-order model represents ambiguity perception, and an outer loss function represents ambiguity attitude. This separation has proved useful in economic and financial applications (Gollier, 2011; Ju and Miao, 2012; Maccheroni et al., 2013). However, its benchmark properties rely on using the expected-loss statistic (which is expected utility when modeling wealth). Direct substitution of different statistics therefore need not preserve the desirable properties, as we show in this paper.

To the best of our knowledge, no existing model can simultaneously accommodate a general pure-risk statistic, represent ambiguity perception, capture ambiguity attitudes separately, and support Bayesian updating. Our goal is to construct ambiguity-sensitive decision functionals that retain these properties while allowing for general statistics.

We fix a statistic representing pure-risk preferences and formulate four properties for decision functionals indexed by a second-order model and an ambiguity attitude. Pure-risk consistency requires that the functional reduces to the statistic when the second-order model is degenerate. Predictive ambiguity neutrality requires evaluation under the predictive model at the ambiguity-neutral benchmark. Attitude monotonicity orders functionals as the DM becomes more ambiguity averse. Strong ambiguity aversion requires monotonicity when second-order beliefs become more dispersed in convex order. Together, these properties separate pure-risk preferences, ambiguity perception, and ambiguity attitude.

Our first set of results clarifies the obstruction created by non-affine statistics. Within the reduction rules considered, second-order averaging satisfies ambiguity neutrality only when the pure-risk statistic is expected loss, and the reduction is the predictive model. Moreover, averaging model-specific expected shortfalls moves in the direction opposite to strong ambiguity aversion as second-order beliefs become more dispersed. We therefore introduce an ambiguity iron that maps a second-order model and an ambiguity attitude to an ambiguity set. Applying the original statistic to every model in this set and taking the worst-case value yields a DRO decision functional. The defining properties of an ambiguity iron ensure the four properties above.

We develop a specific ambiguity iron by distorting second-order models. A concave distortion determines a collection of second-order models dominated by the corresponding distorted probability, and the ambiguity set consists of their predictive first-order models. These distortions represent ambiguity attitudes. We show that this construction defines an ambiguity iron and produces convex, compact ambiguity sets. In a binary-state example, the ambiguity set is an interval of predictive probabilities whose width increases with ambiguity aversion. The example also distinguishes this interval, constructed for decision-making, from a Bayesian credible interval, constructed for posterior coverage.

We next study computation, learning, and model misspecification. We derive alternative formulas for the resulting worst-case functionals and, under a parametric representation, an approximation based on order statistics drawn from the second-order model. We specialize these formulas to optimized certainty equivalents, expected loss, and value-at-risk, and illustrate them in a portfolio problem using four statistics. We then show that posterior concentration, together with continuity of the parametrization in total variation, makes the induced ambiguity sets contract and the decision functionals converge to their pure-risk values. A separate KL-based robustification addresses model misspecification, thereby distinguishing misspecification from ambiguity perception and attitude.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the main objects and the predictive model. Section 3 formulates the four properties and examines the limitations of second-order integral aggregation. Section 4 introduces ambiguity irons, develops the distortion construction, and derives alternative formulas for several statistics. Section 5 studies unambiguous events and acts, including epistemic distributional invariance. Section 6 presents the parametric representation, sampling-based approximation, and numerical illustrations. Section 7 studies Bayesian consistency and model misspecification. The appendices contain the proofs, additional results, and supplementary figures.

2 Preliminaries

Under pure risk, evaluating an act requires both a statistic and a first-order model: the model determines the act’s distribution, while the statistic specifies how to evaluate that distribution. Under ambiguity, a second-order model represents uncertainty about the first-order model. This section introduces these objects and distinguishes their roles in the decision problem. We also define the predictive model obtained by averaging first-order models under the second-order model. This reduction will provide the benchmark for ambiguity-neutral evaluation.

2.1 General notation

Given measurable spaces (Ω,ℱ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F}) and (Ψ,𝒢)(\Psi,\mathcal{G}), a measurable mapping X:Ω→ΨX:\Omega\to\Psi, and a probability measure μ\mu on (Ω,ℱ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F}), the pushforward probability measure X#​μX_{\#}\mu on (Ψ,𝒢)(\Psi,\mathcal{G}) is defined by

X#​μ​(A)=μ⁡(X−1​(A)),A∈𝒢.X_{\#}\mu(A)=\mu(X^{-1}(A)),\penalty\ \penalty\ A\in\mathcal{G}.

A Polish measurable space is a measurable space (Ψ,𝒢)(\Psi,\mathcal{G}) where Ψ\Psi is a Polish topological space and 𝒢\mathcal{G} is its Borel σ\sigma-algebra. We will sometimes denote the Borel σ\sigma-algebra by ℬ⁡(Ψ)\mathcal{B}(\Psi). Given a Polish measurable space (Ψ,𝒢)(\Psi,\mathcal{G}) and a probability measure μ\mu on (Ψ,𝒢)(\Psi,\mathcal{G}), the support of μ\mu is the smallest closed set C⊆ΨC\subseteq\Psi such that μ⁡(C)=1\mu(C)=1. Given a Polish measurable space (Ψ,𝒢)(\Psi,\mathcal{G}) and a sequence of probability measures (μn)n∈ℕ(\mu_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} on (Ψ,𝒢)(\Psi,\mathcal{G}), we say that (μn)n∈ℕ(\mu_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} converges in distribution to some probability measure μ\mu on (Ψ,𝒢)(\Psi,\mathcal{G}), denoted by μn⇒μ\mu_{n}\Rightarrow\mu, if for all continuous and bounded f:Ψ→ℝf:\Psi\to\mathbb{R} we have limn→∞∫Ψf​d​μn=∫Ψf​𝑑μ.\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{\Psi}f\mathrm{d}\mu_{n}=\int_{\Psi}f\mathrm{d}\mu.

2.2 Acts, decision functionals and first-order models

Throughout the paper, we fix a Polish measurable space (Ω,ℱ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F}), which is interpreted as the set of future states of the world. An act is a real-valued measurable function on (Ω,ℱ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F}). In this paper, an act is to be viewed in the loss-profit sense (positive values correspond to losses or bad outcomes). Acts are the main objects of choice studied in this paper and, depending on the context, may represent financial losses, insurable risks, or unrealized endowments. We denote by 𝒳\mathcal{X} the set of all acts, by 𝒳b\mathcal{X}_{b} the set of all bounded acts, by 𝒞\mathcal{C} the set of all continuous acts, and by 𝒞b\mathcal{C}_{b} the set of all continuous bounded acts. Given X,Y∈𝒳X,Y\in\mathcal{X}, we write X≥YX\geq Y if X⁡(ω)≥Y⁡(ω)X(\omega)\geq Y(\omega) for all ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega.

Definition 1.

Let 𝒴⊆𝒳\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathcal{X} contain all constant acts. A decision functional is a map ρ:𝒴→ℝ∪{∞}\rho:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\} for which ρ⁡(X)≥ρ⁡(Y)\rho(X)\geq\rho(Y) whenever X,Y∈𝒴X,Y\in\mathcal{Y} satisfy X≥YX\geq Y, and ρ⁡(c)=c\rho(c)=c for every c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, where cc is identified with the corresponding constant act.

Decision functionals are operational tools for evaluating acts and making decisions. Their numerical output can serve as a stand-alone assessment or as part of an optimization problem. For example, the value of a decision functional may represent an economically meaningful quantity, such as a financial institution’s capital requirement or the premium charged to a policyholder for insuring an uncertain loss. Alternatively, it may rank feasible choices, as in portfolio selection, where one chooses a portfolio by optimizing the value of the decision functional. In economics, decision functionals are used to represent preference relations and, more specifically, represent preferences by a functional that maps acts to their certainty equivalents.

Let Δ\Delta denote the set of probability measures on (Ω,ℱ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F}); we call its elements first-order models. First-order models represent aleatoric uncertainty or pure-risk perception, namely the inherent randomness in which state of the world will be realized. Given X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X} and μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta, we use 𝔼μ​[X]\mathbb{E}^{\mu}[X] to denote the Lebesgue integral of XX under μ\mu. Given X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X}, define the function ψX:Δ→ℝ∪{−∞,∞}\psi_{X}:\Delta\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty,\infty\} by ψX​(μ)=𝔼μ​[X]\psi_{X}(\mu)=\mathbb{E}^{\mu}[X].11 1 When ψX​(μ)\psi_{X}(\mu) is undefined, set it equal to zero. We equip Δ\Delta with the coarsest topology τ\tau where the maps {ψX}X∈𝒞b\{\psi_{X}\}_{X\in\mathcal{C}_{b}} are continuous, i.e., the weak topology. Given μ,ν∈Δ\mu,\nu\in\Delta and λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1], their λ\lambda-mixture, denoted by λ​μ+(1−λ)​ν\lambda\mu+(1-\lambda)\nu, is the first-order model defined by

[λ​μ+(1−λ)​ν]​(A)=λ​μ​(A)+(1−λ)​ν​(A),A∈ℱ.\left[\lambda\mu+(1-\lambda)\nu\right](A)=\lambda\mu(A)+(1-\lambda)\nu(A),\penalty\ \penalty\ A\in\mathcal{F}.

Equipped with this operation, Δ\Delta is a mixture space. Throughout, all references to convex subsets of Δ\Delta and convex, concave, or affine functions defined on Δ\Delta are understood with respect to this mixture structure.

A DM is said to be in the pure-risk setting when they can, either through personal beliefs or statistical inference, identify a unique first-order model μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta that they regard as the probability description governing the realization of future outcomes. Alternatively, we can say that the DM perceives no ambiguity. In this setting, decisions are evaluated using functionals that depend on an act only through its distribution under μ\mu. We now introduce the notation needed to formalize this approach.

Denote by 𝒟\mathcal{D} the set of all Borel probability measures on ℝ\mathbb{R}; we will refer to 𝒟\mathcal{D} as the set of distributions. Given Q∈𝒟Q\in\mathcal{D}, we define the survival function of QQ by SQ​(x)=Q⁡((x,∞))S_{Q}(x)=Q((x,\infty)) for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. For Q,P∈𝒟Q,P\in\mathcal{D}, we say that QQ is larger than PP in stochastic order, denoted by Q≥stPQ\geq_{\mathrm{st}}P, if SQ​(x)≥SP​(x)S_{Q}(x)\geq S_{P}(x) for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. We have that ≥st\geq_{\mathrm{st}} is a partial order on 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Given Q,P∈𝒟Q,P\in\mathcal{D} and λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1], their λ\lambda-mixture, denoted by λ​Q+(1−λ)​P\lambda Q+(1-\lambda)P, is the distribution defined by

[λ​Q+(1−λ)​P]​(B)=λ​Q​(B)+(1−λ)​P​(B),B∈ℬ⁡(ℝ).\left[\lambda Q+(1-\lambda)P\right](B)=\lambda Q(B)+(1-\lambda)P(B),\penalty\ \penalty\ B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}).

Equipped with this operation, 𝒟\mathcal{D} is a mixture space. Throughout, all references to convex, concave, or affine functions defined on 𝒟\mathcal{D} are understood with respect to this mixture structure.

Definition 2.

Let ℰ⊆𝒟\mathcal{E}\subseteq\mathcal{D} contain all Dirac distributions. A statistic is a map γ:ℰ→ℝ∪{∞}\gamma:\mathcal{E}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\} for which γ⁡(Q)≥γ⁡(P)\gamma(Q)\geq\gamma(P) whenever Q,P∈ℰQ,P\in\mathcal{E} satisfy Q≥stPQ\geq_{\mathrm{st}}P, and γ⁡(δc)=c\gamma(\delta_{c})=c for every c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, where δc\delta_{c} denotes the Dirac measure at cc.
