Remark 1.

We use the expected loss convention rather than the usual expected utility because we are working with loss-profit acts. We can switch conventions by taking u⁡(x)=−ℓ⁡(−x).u(x)=-\ell(-x).

Under the distortion gα​(x)=x1−α∧1g_{\alpha}(x)=\frac{x}{1-\alpha}\wedge 1, where α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1), the dual statistic 𝔼gα\mathbb{E}^{g_{\alpha}} coincides with expected shortfall of Acerbi and Tasche (2002), which we denote by ESα\mathrm{ES}_{\alpha}. Expected shortfall is widely used in financial practice and serves as the standard risk measure for market risk within the banking regulatory framework of BCBS (2019). Under the distortion hα=𝟙(1−α,1]h_{\alpha}=\mathds{1}_{(1-\alpha,1]}, where α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), the dual statistic 𝔼hα\mathbb{E}^{h_{\alpha}} coincides with the value-at-risk, which we denote by VaRα\mathrm{VaR}_{\alpha}.

We can now formalize decision-making under pure risk. Recall that, in this setting, the DM identifies a unique first-order model μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta. Given a statistic γ:ℰ→ℝ∪{∞}\gamma:\mathcal{E}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\} also specified by the DM, acts are evaluated using the decision functional

ρ⁡(X)=γ⁡(X|μ):=γ⁡(X#​μ),X∈𝒴,\rho(X)=\gamma(X|\mu):=\gamma(X_{\#}\mu),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{Y},

where the relevant domains 𝒴\mathcal{Y} and ℰ\mathcal{E} are chosen so that the decision functional is well defined. Thus, each act is evaluated solely through the distribution it induces under the DM’s uniquely identified first-order model. Decision functionals produced in this way are said to be law invariant; see McNeil et al. (2015).

2.3 Second-order models and predictive reduction

A natural way to move beyond the pure-risk setting is to replace the uniquely identified first-order model with a collection of models that the DM regards as plausible. The following example illustrates this approach.

Example 1.

In many applications, the DM specifies a collection of plausible first-order models 𝒫⊆Δ\mathcal{P}\subseteq\Delta, called an ambiguity set. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) then evaluates an act according to the worst-case decision functional

ρ⁡(X)=supν∈𝒫γ⁡(X|ν),X∈𝒴,\rho(X)=\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}\gamma(X|\nu),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{Y},

where γ\gamma is the statistic governing the DM’s evaluation in the pure-risk setting. Functionals of this form stem from the maxmin expected utility model of Gilboa and Schmeidler (1989).

In this paper, we take a different approach. Rather than requiring the DM to specify an ambiguity set directly, we represent uncertainty about the appropriate first-order model probabilistically. We equip Δ\Delta with the σ\sigma-algebra generated by τ\tau, denoted by Σ\Sigma. Since (Ω,ℱ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F}) is a Polish measurable space, we know that (Δ,Σ)(\Delta,\Sigma) is a Polish measurable space; see Billingsley (2013, Theorem 6.8). We will use Π\Pi to denote the set of probability measures on (Δ,Σ)(\Delta,\Sigma), which we call the second-order models. Second-order models represent epistemic uncertainty or ambiguity perception, namely uncertainty regarding which first-order model provides the appropriate probabilistic description of the world. In a Bayesian statistical context, both priors and posteriors are second-order models. This is why we use the term “second-order model” rather than “Bayesian prior”: the latter might suggest that our framework applies only before data collection, whereas it also applies after Bayesian updating and moving to the posterior.

For π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, let L1​(π)L^{1}(\pi) denote the set of acts X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X} satisfying ∫Δ𝔼ν​[|X|]​π​(𝑑ν)<∞\int_{\Delta}\mathbb{E}^{\nu}[|X|]\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)<\infty. We verify that ψX\psi_{X} is Σ\Sigma-measurable for all X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X} in Appendix B. For π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, we define the predictive model μπ∈Δ\mu_{\pi}\in\Delta by

μπ​(A)=∫Δν⁡(A)​π​(𝑑ν),A∈ℱ.\mu_{\pi}(A)=\int_{\Delta}\nu(A)\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu),\penalty\ \penalty\ A\in\mathcal{F}.

An application of the dominated-convergence theorem will verify that μπ∈Δ\mu_{\pi}\in\Delta. We verify in Appendix B that, for π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and X∈L1​(π)X\in L^{1}(\pi), we have

∫Δ𝔼⁡(X|ν)​π​(𝑑ν)=∫Δ𝔼ν​[X]​π​(𝑑ν)=𝔼μπ​[X]=𝔼⁡(X|μπ).\int_{\Delta}\mathbb{E}(X|\nu)\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)=\int_{\Delta}\mathbb{E}^{\nu}[X]\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)=\mathbb{E}^{\mu_{\pi}}[X]=\mathbb{E}(X|\mu_{\pi}). (1)
Example 2.

Consider a DM who would evaluate acts using the expected value statistic 𝔼\mathbb{E} in the pure-risk setting, but who perceives ambiguity and represents it through a nondegenerate second-order model π\pi. The DM may aggregate their model-specific evaluations by integrating them with respect to the second-order model π\pi. In the present case, this yields the decision functional

ρ⁡(X)=∫Δ𝔼⁡(X|ν)​π​(𝑑ν)​=(1)​𝔼​(X|μπ),X∈𝒴.\rho(X)=\int_{\Delta}\mathbb{E}(X|\nu)\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)\overset{\eqref{eq:pred}}{=}\mathbb{E}(X|\mu_{\pi}),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{Y}.

The resulting decisions therefore coincide with those of a DM in the pure-risk setting who evaluates acts using the same statistic (the expectation statistic) and takes the predictive model μπ\mu_{\pi} as their unique first-order model. We call this behavior ambiguity neutrality: although the DM perceives ambiguity, their decisions can be represented as if they did not and instead relied on a single first-order model. This reduction relies on the expectation statistic being affine. For a statistic that is not affine, the integral of model-specific evaluations generally cannot be represented by applying the same statistic to the distribution of acts under the predictive model, or, more generally, to any single first-order model.

3 Decision functionals that incorporate second-order models

We now ask how a decision functional should incorporate second-order beliefs when the statistic governing pure-risk preferences is fixed. We first introduce the convex order to compare the dispersion of second-order models. To provide a general basis for assessing different decision functionals, we then formulate four natural properties for such decision functionals. In particular, we identify restrictions on expected-loss aggregation and show why averaging model-specific expected shortfalls can produce a response opposite to ambiguity aversion.

3.1 The convex order on second-order models

We begin by introducing the convex order on second-order models that formalizes the idea that one model represents a greater degree of perceived ambiguity than another. To this end, define the binary relation ≥cx\geq_{\mathrm{cx}} on Π\Pi by

π~≥cxπ⇔∫Δfdπ~≥∫Δfdπ,π~,π∈Π\tilde{\pi}\geq_{\mathrm{cx}}\pi\iff\int_{\Delta}f\mathrm{d}\tilde{\pi}\geq\int_{\Delta}f\mathrm{d}\pi,\penalty\ \penalty\ \tilde{\pi},\pi\in\Pi

for every convex τ\tau-continuous function f:Δ→ℝf:\Delta\to\mathbb{R} for which both integrals are well defined.

Theorem 1.

The binary relation ≥cx\geq_{\mathrm{cx}} is a partial order.

This construction extends the familiar convex order on distributions in the pure-risk setting; see Rothschild and Stiglitz (1970). Whereas the classical convex order compares dispersion over outcomes, this convex order compares the dispersion of second-order models over first-order models. When Δ\Delta is compact, i.e., when Ω\Omega is compact, this relation coincides with the Choquet order discussed in Phelps (2001, Chapter 15). It is also closely connected to Blackwell’s comparison of experiments for a finite family of statistical models. Blackwell (1953) shows that one experiment is more informative than another if and only if the posterior beliefs over these models induced by the former dominate those induced by the latter in convex, or equivalently Choquet, order. Here, we use the same geometric order for a different purpose: a more dispersed second-order model is interpreted as perceiving greater ambiguity.

Proposition 1.

For all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, π≥cxδμπ\pi\geq_{\mathrm{cx}}\delta_{\mu_{\pi}}.

Thus, among all second-order beliefs with predictive model μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta, δμ\delta_{\mu} is the least element under the convex order. Given the second-order model π\pi, although π\pi and δμπ\delta_{\mu_{\pi}} assign the same average probability to every event, the former may distribute probability across several first-order models, whereas the latter places all mass on the single first-order model μπ\mu_{\pi}. The order therefore interprets dispersion around a fixed predictive model as perceived ambiguity.

Example 3.

Consider the binary-state case Ω={ω1,ω2}\Omega=\{\omega_{1},\omega_{2}\}. In this setting, each first-order model μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta can be uniquely identified by p=μ⁡({ω1})p=\mu(\{\omega_{1}\}). Consequently, the set of second-order models can be identified with distributions supported on [0,1][0,1]. Under this identification, the convex order satisfies

π~≥cxπ⇔∫[0,1]h(p)π~(dp)≥∫[0,1]h(p)π(dp)\tilde{\pi}\geq_{\mathrm{cx}}\pi\penalty\ \penalty\ \iff\penalty\ \penalty\ \int_{[0,1]}h(p)\tilde{\pi}(\mathrm{d}p)\geq\int_{[0,1]}h(p)\pi(\mathrm{d}p)

for every continuous convex function h:[0,1]→ℝh:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}. For example, suppose the initial second-order model, or prior, is the standard uniform distribution π0=U⁡(0,1)=Beta⁡(1,1)\pi_{0}=\operatorname{U}(0,1)=\operatorname{Beta}(1,1). Under independent and identically distributed sampling, observing ss realizations of ω1\omega_{1} and ff realizations of ω2\omega_{2} yields, through Bayesian updating, the posterior second-order model Beta⁡(1+s,1+f).\operatorname{Beta}(1+s,1+f). Along the balanced sample path

(ω1,ω1,ω2,ω2,ω1,ω2,ω2,ω1,ω1,ω2),(\omega_{1},\omega_{1},\omega_{2},\omega_{2},\omega_{1},\omega_{2},\omega_{2},\omega_{1},\omega_{1},\omega_{2}),

the posterior distributions after four and ten observations are, respectively, π4=Beta⁡(3,3)\pi_{4}=\operatorname{Beta}(3,3) and π10=Beta⁡(6,6).\pi_{10}=\operatorname{Beta}(6,6). Since π0\pi_{0}, π4\pi_{4}, and π10\pi_{10} all have mean 1/21/2, they induce the same predictive model (1/2,1/2)∈Δ(1/2,1/2)\in\Delta. At the same time, the posterior becomes progressively less dispersed as we collect additional balanced observations; see Figure 1. In particular,

π0≥cxπ4≥cxπ10≥cxδ1/2.\pi_{0}\geq_{\mathrm{cx}}\pi_{4}\geq_{\mathrm{cx}}\pi_{10}\geq_{\mathrm{cx}}\delta_{1/2}.

Thus, along a balanced part of the sample path, Bayesian updating leaves the predictive model unchanged while progressively reducing the second-order model’s dispersion. The common-mean condition is essential for this comparison. In the unbalanced part of the sample path, the posterior mean differs from 1/2, and the resulting posterior need not be comparable under the convex order.

3.2 Four properties

Let 𝒟c\mathcal{D}_{c} denote the set of all Borel probability measures on ℝ\mathbb{R} with compact support. Throughout this section, following the convention in the risk-measure literature, statistics will have domain ℰ=𝒟c\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{D}_{c} and decision functionals will have domain 𝒴=𝒳b\mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{X}_{b}; see Föllmer and Schied (2016).

We begin by identifying general properties that a decision functional incorporating a second-order model should satisfy. Fix a statistic γ\gamma that determines the DM’s decision functional in the absence of ambiguity; we say that γ\gamma encodes the DM’s pure-risk preferences. To introduce ambiguity, we distinguish between the DM’s perception of ambiguity and the DM’s attitude toward it. We represent the former with a second-order model π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, while the latter is represented by an element of a partially ordered set (Λ,≥)(\Lambda,\geq) with least element λ0\lambda_{0}. In this section, we keep the partially ordered set (Λ,≥)(\Lambda,\geq) abstract to keep the discussion general. We recall and introduce specific choices for this structure later.

The order on Λ\Lambda has a comparative interpretation: for λ,λ~∈Λ\lambda,\tilde{\lambda}\in\Lambda, λ≥λ~\lambda\geq\tilde{\lambda} means that the attitude indexed by λ\lambda is at least as ambiguity averse as the attitude indexed by λ~\tilde{\lambda}. The least element λ0\lambda_{0} serves as the ambiguity-neutral benchmark. Thus, the partial order provides a comparative notion of ambiguity aversion, while λ0\lambda_{0} anchors that comparison and thereby yields an absolute classification of ambiguity attitudes. This construction follows the benchmark method underlying the comparative foundations of absolute ambiguity aversion in Ghirardato and Marinacci (2002) and Epstein (2004): ambiguity attitudes are first ordered comparatively, and an attitude is then classified in absolute terms by its position relative to ambiguity neutrality. Because λ0\lambda_{0} is the least element of Λ\Lambda, the present formulation restricts attention to ambiguity-neutral and ambiguity-averse attitudes. The framework can be extended straightforwardly to accommodate ambiguity-seeking attitudes.

We now formulate several desirable properties for decision functionals that combine these three primitives. We therefore consider a family

ρ⁡(⋅,π,λ):𝒳b→ℝ,(π,λ)∈Π×Λ.\rho(\,\cdot\,;\pi,\lambda):\mathcal{X}_{b}\to\mathbb{R},\qquad(\pi,\lambda)\in\Pi\times\Lambda.

This definition of the decision functional separates the DM’s pure-risk preferences, encoded by γ\gamma, from their ambiguity perception π\pi and ambiguity attitude λ\lambda. The first two properties ensure consistency with the pure-risk and ambiguity-neutral benchmarks, while the final two require the functional to respect the comparative orders on ambiguity attitudes and ambiguity perceptions.

Consider the case when the DM’s second-order model is given by δμ\delta_{\mu} for some μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta. Conceptually, this means the DM has no epistemic uncertainty and believes that the first-order model μ\mu correctly describes the aleatoric uncertainty; that is, the DM perceives no ambiguity. In this case, independently of ambiguity attitudes, the DM should make decisions using their pure-risk preferences. This leads us to our first property.

Property 1 (Pure-risk consistency):

For all μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta, λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, and X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b},

ρ⁡(X,δμ,λ)=γ⁡(X|μ).\rho(X;\delta_{\mu},\lambda)=\gamma(X|\mu).

Because the least element λ0\lambda_{0} serves as the benchmark for ambiguity neutrality, we need a canonical procedure to reduce a second-order model to a single first-order model. Motivated by Example 2, we take the corresponding predictive model to provide this canonical reduction. This reduction is common in the literature and has been used in financial risk management (Ardia, 2008; Ardia et al., 2017), actuarial science (Klugman, 1992; Cairns, 2000), and portfolio allocation problems (Kandel and Stambaugh, 1996; Feng and He, 2022). Under ambiguity neutrality, the resulting evaluation should be given by pure-risk preferences after reduction. The following property formalizes these considerations.

Property 2 (Predictive ambiguity neutrality):

For all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b},

ρ⁡(X,π,λ0)=γ⁡(X|μπ).\rho(X;\pi,\lambda_{0})=\gamma(X|\mu_{\pi}).

In the decision-theory literature, one preference relation is more ambiguity averse than another if, for every act (in the profit-loss sense), the certainty equivalent under the former is at most as large as that under the latter. Generalizing this idea to arbitrary decision functionals, while accounting for loss-profit acts, yields the following property.

Property 3 (Attitude monotonicity):

For all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, and λ,λ~∈Λ\lambda,\tilde{\lambda}\in\Lambda satisfying λ≥λ~\lambda\geq\tilde{\lambda},

ρ⁡(X,π,λ)≥ρ⁡(X,π,λ~).\rho(X;\pi,\lambda)\geq\rho(X;\pi,\tilde{\lambda}).

An immediate consequence of Properties 2 and 3 is that, for every π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, and X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b},

ρ⁡(X,π,λ)≥ρ⁡(X,π,λ0)=γ⁡(X|μπ).\rho(X;\pi,\lambda)\geq\rho(X;\pi,\lambda_{0})=\gamma(X|\mu_{\pi}). (2)

Thus, holding the ambiguity perception π\pi fixed, every attitude λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda yields an evaluation at least as conservative as the ambiguity-neutral benchmark. Thus, every attitude λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda is ambiguity averse relative to the predictive benchmark. This follows the benchmark-comparison approach of Ghirardato and Marinacci (2002), while allowing the benchmark to retain a general pure-risk statistic. Properties 2 and 3 thereby give the partially ordered set (Λ,≥)(\Lambda,\geq) its intended interpretation.

The inequality in (2) is a benchmark comparison: under Property 1, it compares the evaluation under the ambiguity perception π\pi to the pure-risk evaluation under the predictive model. In this respect, it parallels the classical notion of weak risk aversion from Pratt (1964) in the pure-risk setting, which compares a distribution of outcomes with the certain outcome equal to its expectation. The passage from weak to strong risk aversion in Rothschild and Stiglitz (1970) replaces this single comparison with monotonicity under the traditional convex order. Since the convex order on Π\Pi provides the corresponding notion of increased dispersion among second-order models, the following property imposes an analogous monotonicity requirement on ambiguity perceptions.

Property 4 (Strong ambiguity aversion):

For all λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, and π,π~∈Π\pi,\tilde{\pi}\in\Pi satisfying π≥cxπ~\pi\geq_{\mathrm{cx}}\tilde{\pi},

ρ⁡(X,π,λ)≥ρ⁡(X,π~,λ).\rho(X;\pi,\lambda)\geq\rho(X;\tilde{\pi},\lambda).

A consequence of Proposition 1 is that Properties 1 and 4 imply the ambiguity-aversion inequality in (2). Therefore, Property 4, in combination with Property 1, strengthens the benchmark notion of ambiguity aversion in the same way that strong risk aversion strengthens weak risk aversion, which motivates the terminology.

In the next subsection, we turn to the decision functionals associated with the smooth model from Klibanoff et al. (2005) and show how the model provides a concrete specification of the partially ordered set (Λ,≥)(\Lambda,\geq) and a family of decision functionals satisfying the above properties. However, we also discuss this model’s inability to represent general pure-risk preferences.

3.3 Limits of second-order integral aggregation

We now provide a first concrete specification of the framework developed in the preceding subsection. In particular, we take the statistic representing the DM’s pure-risk preferences to be an expected-loss statistic. That is, for some loss function hh, we have γ=𝔼h\gamma=\mathbb{E}_{h}. Throughout this subsection, we normalize all loss functions ℓ\ell so that ℓ⁡(0)=0\ell(0)=0 and ℓ⁡(1)=1\ell(1)=1. This normalization entails no loss of generality, since loss functions that differ by a positive affine transformation generate the same expected-loss statistic.

We model ambiguity attitudes by the set

Λh={ϕ∘h:ϕ​ is a convex loss function}.\Lambda_{h}=\left\{\phi\circ h:\phi\text{ is a convex loss function}\right\}.

We equip Λh\Lambda_{h} with the partial order

ℓ≥ℓ~⇔ℓ=ϕ∘ℓ~for some convex loss function ​ϕ.\ell\geq\tilde{\ell}\iff\ell=\phi\circ\tilde{\ell}\penalty\ \penalty\ \text{for some convex loss function }\phi.

It is clear that hh is the least element of Λh\Lambda_{h}.

For each π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and ℓ∈Λh\ell\in\Lambda_{h}, consider the loss-based formulation of the smooth decision functional of Klibanoff et al. (2005),

ρ⁡(X,π,ℓ)=ℓ−1​(∫Δℓ⁡(𝔼h​(X|ν))​π​(𝑑ν)),X∈𝒳b.\rho(X;\pi,\ell)=\ell^{-1}\left(\int_{\Delta}\ell\left(\mathbb{E}_{h}(X|\nu)\right)\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)\right),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}. (3)

These decision functionals have been used extensively in the literature (Gollier, 2011; Ju and Miao, 2012; Maccheroni et al., 2013) because they clearly separate pure risk, ambiguity perception, and ambiguity attitude. The next result shows that this family of decision functionals realizes all the properties introduced in the preceding subsection.

Proposition 2.

The family of decision functionals defined by (3) satisfies Properties 1–4.

Although the smooth model provides a concrete family satisfying Properties 1–4, this conclusion depends on the assumption that the pure-risk preferences are given by an expected-loss statistic. To see this, observe that

∫Δh⁡(𝔼h​(X|ν))​π​(𝑑ν)=∫Δ𝔼⁡(h⁡(X)|ν)​π​(𝑑ν)​=(1)​𝔼​(h⁡(X)|μπ),X∈𝒳b.\int_{\Delta}h\left(\mathbb{E}_{h}(X|\nu)\right)\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)=\int_{\Delta}\mathbb{E}\left(h(X)|\nu\right)\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)\overset{\eqref{eq:pred}}{=}\mathbb{E}(h(X)|\mu_{\pi}),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}.

Therefore, Property 2 relies on the fact that the statistic is expected loss. Second, composing the affine map μ↦𝔼⁡(h⁡(X)|μ)\mu\mapsto\mathbb{E}(h(X)|\mu), where X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, with a convex loss function produces a convex function on first-order models, which allows the smooth functional to respect the convex order on second-order models and thereby satisfy Property 4. A general statistic need not have either property, as we show below.

This restriction is important in applications because the statistic governing pure-risk preferences should be decoupled from ambiguity perception and attitude. For example, under the perception of no ambiguity, a bank may be required to calculate regulatory capital requirements using expected shortfall. Therefore, a Bayesian extension of expected shortfall should incorporate a second-order model while still reducing to expected shortfall both when the DM perceives no ambiguity (Property 1) and when the DM is ambiguity neutral (Property 2). It should also satisfy Properties 3 and 4 if we want to consider ambiguity-averse behavior.

To illustrate the above points more concretely, if one wanted to create a Bayesian extension of the expected shortfall, a natural first attempt would be to replace the 𝔼h\mathbb{E}_{h} in (3) with ESα\mathrm{ES}_{\alpha}. This substitution is appealing because decision functionals originating in decision theory are often adapted to other areas by replacing the expected-loss statistic with the relevant domain-specific statistic; the derivation of the DRO paradigm from the maxmin expected utility model of Gilboa and Schmeidler (1989) is a prominent example. However, such a direct substitution is incompatible with ambiguity neutrality, as the following theorem shows.

One might wonder whether this incompatibility depends on reducing each second-order model to its predictive first-order model. To show that the result is independent of this particular choice of reduction, we consider a broader class of mappings from second-order models to first-order models.

Definition 3.

A mapping ℜ:Π→Δ\mathfrak{R}:\Pi\to\Delta is called a reduction rule if, for every π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, A∈ℱA\in\mathcal{F}, and a∈[0,1]a\in[0,1], if π(ν∈Δ:ν(A)=a)=1\pi(\nu\in\Delta:\nu(A)=a)=1 then [ℜ​(π)]​(A)=a.\left[\mathfrak{R}(\pi)\right](A)=a.

The predictive reduction is a particular reduction rule, but Definition 3 permits more general reductions of a second-order model to a first-order model. The following theorem shows that this additional freedom does not rescue the second-order aggregation procedure found in the smooth model. Indeed, among all statistics and all reduction rules, the only case in which loss-based second-order aggregation can always be represented as evaluation of the same statistic under a reduced first-order model is the expected-loss statistic together with the predictive reduction.

Theorem 2.

Assume that Ω\Omega is uncountable. Let ℓ\ell be a loss function, γ\gamma be a statistic, and ℜ:Π→Δ\mathfrak{R}:\Pi\to\Delta be a reduction rule. Then the following statements are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    For every π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b},

    ℓ−1​(∫Δℓ⁡(γ⁡(X|ν))​π​(𝑑ν))=γ⁡(X|ℜ⁡(π)).\ell^{-1}\left(\int_{\Delta}\ell\left(\gamma(X|\nu)\right)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)\right)=\gamma\left(X|\mathfrak{R}(\pi)\right). (4)
  2. (ii)

    The statistic γ\gamma is the expected-loss statistic 𝔼ℓ\mathbb{E}_{\ell} and ℜ\mathfrak{R} is the predictive reduction.

Theorem 2 therefore shows that the expected-loss statistic is not incidental to the smooth model: it is the unique pure-risk statistic compatible with this form of second-order aggregation and first-order reduction. Consequently, accommodating general statistics while preserving ambiguity neutrality requires a different procedure.

Finally, expected shortfall has another distinctive feature under second-order averaging. For X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X}, define the mapping ιX:Δ→𝒟\iota_{X}:\Delta\to\mathcal{D} by ιX​(μ)=X#​μ\iota_{X}(\mu)=X_{\#}\mu. We verify in Appendix C that, for every X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, the mapping ESα∘ιX\mathrm{ES}_{\alpha}\circ\iota_{X} is Σ\Sigma-measurable.

Proposition 3.

If π~,π∈Π\tilde{\pi},\pi\in\Pi satisfy π~≥cxπ\tilde{\pi}\geq_{\mathrm{cx}}\pi, then

∫ΔESα​(X|ν)​π~​(𝑑ν)≤∫ΔESα​(X|ν)​π​(𝑑ν),X∈𝒳b.\int_{\Delta}\mathrm{ES}_{\alpha}(X|\nu)\tilde{\pi}(\mathrm{d}\nu)\leq\int_{\Delta}\mathrm{ES}_{\alpha}(X|\nu)\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}.

This inequality goes in the opposite direction of Property 4. In particular, by Proposition 1,

∫ΔESα​(X|ν)​π​(𝑑ν)≤ESα​(X|μπ),X∈𝒳b.\int_{\Delta}\mathrm{ES}_{\alpha}(X|\nu)\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)\leq\mathrm{ES}_{\alpha}(X|\mu_{\pi}),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}.

Consequently, if banks were permitted to incorporate a second-order model in calculating regulatory capital requirements, they would have an incentive to adopt a highly dispersed second-order model and compute the average expected shortfall under that model, rather than determine regulatory capital requirements based on the predictive model. Therefore, the resulting decision functional will incentivize ambiguity-seeking behavior. From a regulatory perspective, this is highly problematic, as banks should exhibit ambiguity aversion to strengthen the financial system’s resilience during periods of heightened economic ambiguity. This observation is not unique to expected shortfall, as any concave statistic (see Acciaio and Svindland (2013); Delage et al. (2019); Wang et al. (2020)) would have the same interpretation.

4 Ambiguity irons

The limitations of second-order integral aggregation motivate a construction in which beliefs and ambiguity attitudes determine an ambiguity set. We call this transformation an ambiguity iron. The resulting decision functional is a worst-case decision functional (see Example 1) under this ambiguity set. Conditions on the transformation ensure that this decision functional satisfies the four properties introduced above. We then construct an ambiguity iron using distortions of second-order models, study the resulting ambiguity sets, and derive alternative formulas for the statistic when it is given by an optimized certainty equivalent, expected loss, or value-at-risk.

4.1 General definition

In this section, we define ambiguity irons. Ambiguity irons transform second-order models into an ambiguity set. As we discuss later, this transformation accounts for ambiguity attitudes. We will use ambiguity irons to construct decision functionals within the DRO paradigm. We will see that this idea naturally leads to decision functionals that satisfy Properties 1–4.

Let (Λ,≥)(\Lambda,\geq) be a partially ordered set with least element λ0\lambda_{0}. As in the preceding sections, Λ\Lambda indexes ambiguity attitudes, the partial order ≥\geq represents comparative ambiguity aversion, and λ0\lambda_{0} serves as the ambiguity-neutral benchmark. The defining properties of an ambiguity iron stated below parallel Properties 1–4 and admit analogous interpretations.

Definition 4.

A map 𝒰:Π×Λ→2Δ\mathcal{U}:\Pi\times\Lambda\to 2^{\Delta} is called an ambiguity iron if it satisfies:

  1. –

    Degeneracy consistency: for all μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta and λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, 𝒰⁡(δμ,λ)={μ}.\mathcal{U}(\delta_{\mu},\lambda)=\{\mu\}.

  2. –

    Predictive ambiguity neutrality: for all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, 𝒰⁡(π,λ0)={μπ}.\mathcal{U}(\pi,\lambda_{0})=\{\mu_{\pi}\}.

  3. –

    Attitude monotonicity: for all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and λ,λ~∈Λ\lambda,\tilde{\lambda}\in\Lambda satisfying λ≥λ~\lambda\geq\tilde{\lambda}, 𝒰⁡(π,λ)⊇𝒰⁡(π,λ~).\mathcal{U}(\pi,\lambda)\supseteq\mathcal{U}(\pi,\tilde{\lambda}).

  4. –

    Strong ambiguity aversion: for all λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda and π,π~∈Π\pi,\tilde{\pi}\in\Pi satisfying π≥cxπ~\pi\geq_{\mathrm{cx}}\tilde{\pi}, 𝒰⁡(π,λ)⊇𝒰⁡(π~,λ).\mathcal{U}(\pi,\lambda)\supseteq\mathcal{U}(\tilde{\pi},\lambda).

A concept similar to ambiguity irons appears in Gajdos et al. (2008), where the authors introduce selected probability-possibility sets. Like our ambiguity irons, their selected probability-possibility sets take an object representing ambiguity perception as an input and output an ambiguity set. The key distinction lies in how they model ambiguity perception: we use a second-order model as input, whereas they use the initial structured ambiguity set, i.e., the ambiguity set consistent with the constraints of the decision problem. In that work, they likewise interpret this reduction as encoding attitudes toward ambiguity.

Ambiguity sets constructed from second-order models have recently been discussed in Dellaporta et al. (2025); Dellaporta et al. (2026). Taking Λ=[0,∞)\Lambda=[0,\infty), these papers introduce the mappings 𝒰PP\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{PP}} and 𝒰PE\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{PE}}, both with domain Π×[0,∞)\Pi\times[0,\infty), defined by

𝒰PP​(π,ϵ)\displaystyle\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{PP}}(\pi,\epsilon) ={μ∈Δ|KL⁡(μ|μπ)≤ϵ}\displaystyle=\{\mu\in\Delta\penalty\ |\penalty\ \mathrm{KL}(\mu|\mu_{\pi})\leq\epsilon\}
𝒰PE​(π,ϵ)\displaystyle\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{PE}}(\pi,\epsilon) ={μ∈Δ|∫ΔKL⁡(μ|ν)​π​(𝑑ν)≤ϵ},\displaystyle=\left\{\mu\in\Delta\penalty\ \bigg|\penalty\ \int_{\Delta}\mathrm{KL}(\mu|\nu)\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)\leq\epsilon\right\},

where KL\mathrm{KL} denotes the Kullback–Leibler divergence. We verify in Appendix D that the mapping ν↦KL⁡(μ|ν)\nu\mapsto\mathrm{KL}(\mu|\nu) is Σ\Sigma-measurable for all μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta. The mappings 𝒰PP\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{PP}} and 𝒰PE\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{PE}} have a similar structure to our ambiguity irons, but neither satisfies all the properties of an ambiguity iron. For example, neither satisfies degeneracy consistency. This failure follows from the fact that 𝒰PP\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{PP}} and 𝒰PE\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{PE}} were introduced to address problems related to model misspecification; see Shapiro et al. (2023) and Cerreia-Vioglio et al. (2026). We will discuss model misspecification later in Section 7.2.

Given a statistic γ\gamma, an ambiguity iron 𝒰\mathcal{U}, π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, and λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, define the worst-case decision functional ρ⁡(⋅,π,λ):𝒳b→ℝ\rho(\,\cdot\,;\pi,\lambda):\mathcal{X}_{b}\to\mathbb{R} by

ρ⁡(X,π,λ)=supν∈𝒰⁡(π,λ)γ⁡(X|ν),X∈𝒳b.\rho(X;\pi,\lambda)=\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{U}(\pi,\lambda)}\gamma(X|\nu),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}. (5)

The family of decision functionals defined in (5) satisfies Properties 1–4. In the next subsection, we provide a tractable example of an ambiguity iron.

4.2 The distortion ambiguity iron

Let ΛD\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}} denote the set of all continuous concave distortion functions. Define the partial order ≥\geq on ΛD\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}} by pointwise dominance: g≥g~g\geq\tilde{g} if and only if g⁡(x)≥g~​(x)​ for all ​x∈[0,1].g(x)\geq\tilde{g}(x)\text{ for all }x\in[0,1]. The partially ordered set (ΛD,≥)(\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}},\geq) has a least element g0g_{0}, which is given by g0​(x)=xg_{0}(x)=x for all x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1]. Given π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and g∈ΛDg\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}, define the collection of second-order models

ℛ⁡(π,g)={ξ∈Π|ξ⁡(B)≤g⁡(π⁡(B))​for all ​B∈Σ}.\mathcal{R}(\pi,g)=\left\{\xi\in\Pi\penalty\ |\penalty\ \xi(B)\leq g(\pi(B))\ \text{for all }B\in\Sigma\right\}.

Since gg is concave and continuous, the capacity g∘πg\circ\pi is submodular and continuous; see Marinacci and Montrucchio (2004). Furthermore, this implies ℛ⁡(π,g)≠∅\mathcal{R}(\pi,g)\neq\varnothing and

max⁡∫Δξ∈ℛ⁡(π,g)⁡f⁡(ν)​ξ​(𝑑ν)=∫0∞g⁡(π⁡(f>x))​𝑑x+∫−∞0(g⁡(π⁡(f>x))−1)​𝑑x=:∫Δf⁡(ν)​g∘π⁡(𝑑ν),\max_{\xi\in\mathcal{R}(\pi,g)}\int_{\Delta}f(\nu)\xi(\mathrm{d}\nu)=\int_{0}^{\infty}g(\pi(f>x))\mathrm{d}x+\int_{-\infty}^{0}(g(\pi(f>x))-1)\mathrm{d}x=:\int_{\Delta}f(\nu)g\circ\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu), (6)

where f:Δ→ℝf:\Delta\to\mathbb{R} is Σ\Sigma-measurable, whenever the right-hand side is well-defined (i.e., at least one of the two integrals is finite). The right-hand side of (6) is the Choquet integral; see Denneberg (1994).

Define the mapping 𝒮:Π×ΛD→2Δ\mathcal{S}:\Pi\times\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}\to 2^{\Delta} by

𝒮⁡(π,g)={μξ|ξ∈ℛ⁡(π,g)}.\mathcal{S}(\pi,g)=\left\{\mu_{\xi}\penalty\ |\penalty\ \xi\in\mathcal{R}(\pi,g)\right\}. (7)
Theorem 3.

The mapping 𝒮\mathcal{S} from (7) is an ambiguity iron.

Before turning to applications of the distortion ambiguity iron, we record two useful structural properties of the induced ambiguity sets.

Proposition 4.

Given π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and g∈ΛDg\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}, we have that 𝒮⁡(π,g)\mathcal{S}(\pi,g) is convex and τ\tau-compact.

Example 4.

Assume the same set-up as Example 3. For β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1), consider the distortion function gβ​(x)=x1−β∧1g_{\beta}(x)=\frac{x}{1-\beta}\wedge 1. Since gβ≥gβ′g_{\beta}\geq g_{\beta^{\prime}} if and only if β≥β′\beta\geq\beta^{\prime}, the parameter β\beta corresponds to ambiguity-aversion attitudes, with larger values of β\beta corresponding to greater ambiguity aversion. For a,b>0a,b>0, denote by πa,b\pi_{a,b} the second-order model given by Beta⁡(a,b)\operatorname{Beta}(a,b). Since 𝒮⁡(πa,b,gβ)\mathcal{S}(\pi_{a,b},g_{\beta}) is compact and convex by Proposition 4, it follows that

𝒮⁡(a,b,β):=𝒮⁡(πa,b,gβ)=[pl​(a,b,β),pu​(a,b,β)],where​ 0≤pl​(a,b,β)≤pu​(a,b,β)≤1.\mathcal{S}(a,b,\beta):=\mathcal{S}(\pi_{a,b},g_{\beta})=[p_{l}(a,b,\beta),p_{u}(a,b,\beta)],\penalty\ \penalty\ \text{where}\penalty\ \penalty\ 0\leq p_{l}(a,b,\beta)\leq p_{u}(a,b,\beta)\leq 1.

We verify in the Appendix D that

pl​(a,b,β)=11−β​∫01−βVaRα​(πa,b)​𝑑αandpu​(a,b,β)=11−β​∫β1VaRα​(πa,b)​𝑑α.p_{l}(a,b,\beta)=\frac{1}{1-\beta}\int_{0}^{1-\beta}\mathrm{VaR}_{\alpha}(\pi_{a,b})\mathrm{d}\alpha\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \text{and}\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ p_{u}(a,b,\beta)=\frac{1}{1-\beta}\int_{\beta}^{1}\mathrm{VaR}_{\alpha}(\pi_{a,b})\mathrm{d}\alpha.

In the simple case when a=b=1a=b=1, we have that π1,1=U⁡(0,1)\pi_{1,1}=\operatorname{U}(0,1) and a simple calculation shows that

𝒮⁡(1,1,β)=[1−β2,1+β2].\mathcal{S}(1,1,\beta)=\left[\frac{1-\beta}{2},\frac{1+\beta}{2}\right].

An important interval to compare with the ambiguity-iron interval is the standard Bayesian credible interval for beta distributions. This interval is given by

𝒬⁡(a,b,β)=[VaR(1−β)/2​(πa,b),VaR(1+β)/2​(πa,b)].\mathcal{Q}(a,b,\beta)=\left[\mathrm{VaR}_{(1-\beta)/2}(\pi_{a,b}),\mathrm{VaR}_{(1+\beta)/2}(\pi_{a,b})\right].

The Bayesian credible interval has the benefit that πa,b​(p∈𝒬⁡(a,b,β))=β\pi_{a,b}(p\in\mathcal{Q}(a,b,\beta))=\beta. In the case where a=b=1a=b=1, we have that 𝒮⁡(1,1,β)=𝒬⁡(1,1,β)\mathcal{S}(1,1,\beta)=\mathcal{Q}(1,1,\beta). Figure 2 reports the results of a numerical experiment in which we begin with the uniform prior Beta⁡(1,1)\operatorname{Beta}(1,1), observe a sequence of independent realizations generated by the fixed first-order model μ=(0.6,0.4)\mu=(0.6,0.4), and update the posterior after each observation. At each stage, we plot the corresponding predictive model, the interval generated by the ambiguity iron, and the associated Bayesian credible interval, all constructed using β=0.6\beta=0.6. The two constructions produce similar intervals in this simple binary setting, with only minor visible differences. Rather than diminishing the value of the ambiguity-iron approach, this similarity shows that it recovers behavior consistent with familiar Bayesian methods in a setting where those methods are easy to implement. In higher-dimensional problems, optimization over Bayesian credible regions can become computationally difficult. The representations developed in Section 6 provide sampling-based methods for evaluating the decision functionals induced by the distortion ambiguity iron.

4.3 Alternative formulas

In this section, we present alternative representations of (5) for several families of statistics. We also allow the decision functionals to be defined on domains larger than 𝒳b\mathcal{X}_{b}, which is more suitable for the numerical analysis in Section 6. To accommodate this larger domain, let 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} denote the subset of 𝒟\mathcal{D} consisting of distributions with finite first moment, which will serve as the domain of the statistics considered in this section.

A key consideration in the results that follow is ensuring the required integrability conditions hold when changing first-order models. Accordingly, we denote by ΛD∗\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}^{*} the subset of ΛD\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}} consisting of distortion functions gg for which there exists a∈ℕa\in\mathbb{N} such that

g⁡(x)≤a​x,x∈[0,1].g(x)\leq ax,\qquad x\in[0,1].

Optimized certainty equivalents.

We first derive an alternative formula when the statistic is an optimized certainty equivalent; see Ben-Tal and Teboulle (2007). Let h:ℝ→ℝh:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be convex, continuous, and increasing satisfying h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0 and h⁡(x)≥xh(x)\geq x for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. Define the statistic

OCEh​(Q)=infm∈ℝ{m+∫ℝh⁡(x−m)​Q​(𝑑x)},Q∈𝒟1.\mathrm{OCE}_{h}(Q)=\inf_{m\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{m+\int_{\mathbb{R}}h(x-m)Q(\mathrm{d}x)\right\},\penalty\ \penalty\ Q\in\mathcal{D}_{1}.

The expected shortfall statistic ESα\mathrm{ES}_{\alpha} provides a classic example of an optimized certainty equivalent. It arises when h⁡(x)=x+/(1−α)h(x)=x_{+}/(1-\alpha) for some α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1). In this case, the optimized certainty equivalent representation coincides with the well-known formulation of expected shortfall in Rockafellar and Uryasev (2002).

We have the following alternative formula for (5) under the distortion ambiguity iron when the statistic is given by an optimized certainty equivalent.

Theorem 4.

Let π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, g∈ΛD∗g\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}^{*}, and X∈L1​(π)X\in L^{1}(\pi). If h⁡(X−m)∈L1​(π)h(X-m)\in L^{1}(\pi) for every m∈ℝm\in\mathbb{R}, then

supν∈𝒮⁡(π,g)OCEh​(X|ν)=infm∈ℝ{m+∫Δ𝔼ν​[h⁡(X−m)]​g∘π⁡(𝑑ν)}.\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{S}(\pi,g)}\mathrm{OCE}_{h}(X|\nu)=\inf_{m\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{m+\int_{\Delta}\mathbb{E}^{\nu}[h(X-m)]\,g\circ\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)\right\}.

Theorem 4 is a Bayesian counterpart to the robust-optimized certainty-equivalent constructions studied in Bartl et al. (2020) and Wu et al. (2024). Bartl et al. (2020) replace the reference expectation in the classical OCE with a nonlinear expectation and derive tractable representations when model uncertainty is described, in particular, through Wasserstein penalties around a fixed baseline first-order model. Wu et al. (2024) consider the more general functional

infm∈ℝ{m+ρ⁡(h⁡(X−m))},\inf_{m\in\mathbb{R}}\{m+\rho(h(X-m))\},

where ρ\rho is a convex risk measure. Theorem 4 shows that, under the distortion ambiguity iron, the worst-case OCE admits a representation with a similar form to those derived in these works. The main distinction is that these papers impose the ambiguity specifications directly through ambiguity sets or penalty functions; they do not generate them from a second-order model over first-order models.

Expected loss.

The expected-loss case admits a particularly simple representation, which can be approximated using Theorem 7. In contrast to optimized certainty equivalents, it does not require an additional optimization: after evaluating the transformed loss under each first-order model, the resulting values can be aggregated directly through the Choquet integral. Let ℓ:ℝ→ℝ\ell:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be a convex loss function, π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, g∈ΛD∗g\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}^{*}, and X∈L1​(π)X\in L^{1}(\pi) such that ℓ​(X)∈L1​(π)\ell(X)\in L^{1}(\pi). We have

supν∈𝒮⁡(π,g)𝔼ℓ​(X|ν)=ℓ−1​(∫Δ𝔼ν​[ℓ⁡(X)]​g∘π⁡(𝑑ν)).\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{S}(\pi,g)}\mathbb{E}_{\ell}(X|\nu)=\ell^{-1}\left(\int_{\Delta}\mathbb{E}^{\nu}[\ell(X)]g\circ\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)\right).

This decision functional is the loss-based certainty-equivalent version of the second-order dual expected utility model of Giraud (2014), in which model-specific expected losses are aggregated using the dual model of Yaari (1987) rather than through a nonlinear second-order utility.

This representation also connects directly to the Bayesian risk optimization framework of Wu et al. (2018). When the second-order model π\pi is taken to be a posterior distribution, the quantity inside the inverse of the loss function is a functional applied to the posterior distribution of model-specific expected losses, of the type studied in that work.

When the loss function is given by ℓη​(x)=eη​x\ell_{\eta}(x)=e^{\eta x} for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, where η>0\eta>0, the statistic 𝔼ℓη\mathbb{E}_{\ell_{\eta}} coincides with the entropic risk measure ERη\mathrm{ER}_{\eta}; see Föllmer and Schied (2002).

Value-at-risk.

The final statistic for which we derive an alternative representation is value-at-risk. Unlike the preceding statistics, we cannot obtain its worst-case evaluation by calculating a worst-case expected loss. Theorem 5 shows that worst-case value-at-risk is computed by first aggregating the model-specific survival functions and then inverting the resulting aggregate, similarly to Liu et al. (2024).

Theorem 5.

Let π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, g∈ΛDg\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}, and α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1). Then

supν∈𝒮⁡(π,g)VaRα​(X|ν)=inf{x∈ℝ:∫Δν⁡(X>x)​g∘π⁡(𝑑ν)≤1−α},X∈𝒳.\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{S}(\pi,g)}\mathrm{VaR}_{\alpha}(X|\nu)=\inf\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}:\int_{\Delta}\nu(X>x)\,g\circ\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)\leq 1-\alpha\right\},\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}.

Notably, unlike the preceding expected-loss-based formulas, Theorem 5 does not require a moment condition on acts. The worst-case value-at-risk remains finite because the distorted survival function converges to zero as the threshold increases.

5 Unambiguous events and unambiguous acts

A nondegenerate second-order model need not make every act ambiguous. Different first-order models may disagree about some events while inducing the same distribution for a particular act. This section identifies acts and events that are unambiguous in this sense. For the distortion ambiguity iron, we show that evaluating such an act reduces to applying the statistic to its common distribution, independently of ambiguity attitude. We also establish an invariance result for acts inducing the same epistemic distributional beliefs. These results clarify which uncertainty the decision functional responds to and explain the treatment of unambiguous positions in the numerical examples that follow.

Let τ𝒟\tau_{\mathcal{D}} denote the topology on 𝒟\mathcal{D} associated with convergence in distribution and let Σ𝒟\Sigma_{\mathcal{D}} be the σ\sigma-algebra generated by τ𝒟\tau_{\mathcal{D}}. It follows that (𝒟,Σ𝒟)(\mathcal{D},\Sigma_{\mathcal{D}}) is a Polish measurable space.

Proposition 5.

Given X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X}, the mapping ιX:Δ→𝒟\iota_{X}:\Delta\to\mathcal{D} is Σ/Σ𝒟\Sigma/\Sigma_{\mathcal{D}}-measurable.

Given π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X}, the probability measure (ιX)#​π(\iota_{X})_{\#}\pi on (𝒟,Σ𝒟)(\mathcal{D},\Sigma_{\mathcal{D}}) represents the epistemic belief regarding the distribution of XX. Given π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, define

ℭ⁡(π)={X∈𝒳:(ιX)#​π=δQ​ for some ​Q∈𝒟}.\mathfrak{C}(\pi)=\{X\in\mathcal{X}:(\iota_{X})_{\#}\pi=\delta_{Q}\text{ for some }Q\in\mathcal{D}\}.

Intuitively, ℭ⁡(π)\mathfrak{C}(\pi) represents the set of acts with an unambiguous distribution under the second-order model π∈Π\pi\in\Pi. Additionally, for π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, define the set

𝔘⁡(π)={A∈ℱ:𝟙A∈ℭ⁡(π)}.\mathfrak{U}(\pi)=\{A\in\mathcal{F}:\mathds{1}_{A}\in\mathfrak{C}(\pi)\}.

We can view 𝔘⁡(π)\mathfrak{U}(\pi) as the set of unambiguous events.

Proposition 6.

Given π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, the set 𝔘⁡(π)\mathfrak{U}(\pi) is a λ\lambda-system, that is,

  1. (i)

    Ω∈𝔘⁡(π)\Omega\in\mathfrak{U}(\pi);

  2. (ii)

    if A∈𝔘⁡(π)A\in\mathfrak{U}(\pi) then Ac∈𝔘⁡(π)A^{c}\in\mathfrak{U}(\pi);

  3. (iii)

    if the sequence (An)n∈ℕ⊆𝔘⁡(π)(A_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathfrak{U}(\pi) is pairwise disjoint then ⋃n=1∞An∈𝔘⁡(π)\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_{n}\in\mathfrak{U}(\pi).

Moreover, ℭ⁡(π)={X∈𝒳|X−1​(B)∈𝔘⁡(π)​ for all ​B∈ℬ⁡(ℝ)}\mathfrak{C}(\pi)=\{X\in\mathcal{X}\penalty\ |\penalty\ X^{-1}(B)\in\mathfrak{U}(\pi)\text{ for all }B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\}.

The use of a λ\lambda-system for unambiguous events is common in the literature; see Zhang (2002), Marinacci (2002), Epstein (2004), and Van Oosten and Wang (2025). Given π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and X∈ℭ⁡(π)X\in\mathfrak{C}(\pi), let QXπ∈𝒟Q_{X}^{\pi}\in\mathcal{D} denote the distribution satisfying (ιX)#​π=δQXπ(\iota_{X})_{\#}\pi=\delta_{Q_{X}^{\pi}}. The following proposition confirms that, when an act has an unambiguous distribution, the decision functional given in (5) under the distortion ambiguity iron reduces to calculating the statistic on this unambiguous distribution.

Proposition 7.

Let γ\gamma be a statistic, π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, and g∈ΛDg\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}. We have that

supν∈𝒮⁡(π,g)γ⁡(X|ν)=γ⁡(QXπ),X∈ℭ⁡(π).\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{S}(\pi,g)}\gamma(X|\nu)=\gamma(Q_{X}^{\pi}),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathfrak{C}(\pi).

The final result states that the decision functionals in (5) under the distortion ambiguity iron are invariant to epistemic distributional beliefs.

Theorem 6.

Let π,ξ∈Π\pi,\xi\in\Pi, g∈ΛDg\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}, and γ\gamma be a statistic. We have

(ιX)#​π=(ιY)#​ξ⟹supμ∈𝒮⁡(π,g)γ⁡(X|μ)=supμ∈𝒮⁡(ξ,g)γ⁡(Y|μ),X,Y∈𝒳.(\iota_{X})_{\#}\pi=(\iota_{Y})_{\#}\xi\implies\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal{S}(\pi,g)}\gamma(X|\mu)=\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal{S}(\xi,g)}\gamma(Y|\mu),\penalty\ \penalty\ X,Y\in\mathcal{X}.

It seems natural that any Bayesian decision model should be invariant to epistemic distributional beliefs. This requirement is analogous to law invariance in the pure-risk setting: evaluation should depend only on distributional beliefs.

6 Parametrization and computation

We now turn to calculating the proposed decision functionals from samples of the second-order model. We first introduce a parametrization that represents first-order models by parameters without changing the ambiguity-set construction. We then show how to approximate the Choquet integrals appearing in the earlier representations using weighted order statistics. The convergence result applies to sampling schemes satisfying the stated averaging condition, including direct sampling and suitable MCMC schemes. Finally, portfolio examples illustrate how to implement these formulas and how ambiguity perception and ambiguity attitude affect the evaluation of financial positions.

6.1 Parametrization

To make these ideas more tractable, we work with the Polish measurable space (Θ,𝒜)(\Theta,\mathcal{A}), interpreted as the parameter space. We also have a mapping 𝔓:Θ→Δ\mathfrak{P}:\Theta\to\Delta, called a parametrization. We will assume that

  1. (1)

    𝔓\mathfrak{P} is 𝒜/Σ\mathcal{A}/\Sigma-measurable;

  2. (2)

    θ=θ~⇔𝔓⁡(θ)=𝔓⁡(θ~)\theta=\tilde{\theta}\iff\mathfrak{P}(\theta)=\mathfrak{P}(\tilde{\theta});

  3. (3)

    𝒜=𝔓−1​(Σ).\mathcal{A}=\mathfrak{P}^{-1}(\Sigma).

It is well-known (see Bertsekas and Shreve (1996, Proposition 7.25)) that Condition (1) is equivalent to requiring that, for all A∈ℱA\in\mathcal{F}, the mapping θ↦[𝔓​(θ)]​(A)\theta\mapsto[\mathfrak{P}(\theta)](A) is 𝒜\mathcal{A}-measurable. In other words, 𝔓\mathfrak{P} is a probability kernel. Condition (3) may be hard to check in practice; however, by the Lusin-Souslin theorem (Kechris 2012, Theorem 15.1), if Condition (2) holds and 𝔓\mathfrak{P} is continuous, Condition (3) holds.

We denote by Δ⁡(Θ)\Delta(\Theta) the set of probability measures on (Θ,𝒜)(\Theta,\mathcal{A}). Through the parametrization, an element π∈Δ⁡(Θ)\pi\in\Delta(\Theta) induces a second-order model 𝔓#​π\mathfrak{P}_{\#}\pi. Therefore, we may view Δ⁡(Θ)\Delta(\Theta) as a subset of second-order models. Conceptually, there are two different ways to define ambiguity sets given π∈Δ⁡(Θ)\pi\in\Delta(\Theta) and g∈ΛDg\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}. The first is to take 𝒮⁡(𝔓#​π,g)\mathcal{S}(\mathfrak{P}_{\#}\pi,g). The second begins by defining

ℛ0​(π,g)={ξ∈Δ⁡(Θ)|ξ⁡(A)≤g⁡(π⁡(A))​for all​A∈𝒜},\mathcal{R}_{0}(\pi,g)=\left\{\xi\in\Delta(\Theta)\penalty\ |\penalty\ \xi(A)\leq g(\pi(A))\penalty\ \text{for all}\penalty\ A\in\mathcal{A}\right\},

and then defining the ambiguity set 𝒮0​(π,g)\mathcal{S}_{0}(\pi,g) as the set of all first-order models given by

μ⁡(A)=∫Θμθ​(A)​ξ​(𝑑θ),A∈ℱ,\mu(A)=\int_{\Theta}\mu_{\theta}(A)\xi(\mathrm{d}\theta),\penalty\ \penalty\ A\in\mathcal{F},

for some ξ∈ℛ0​(π,g)\xi\in\mathcal{R}_{0}(\pi,g), where μθ=𝔓⁡(θ)\mu_{\theta}=\mathfrak{P}(\theta) for all θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta. The following proposition confirms that these methods produce the same ambiguity set.

Proposition 8.

Let π∈Δ⁡(Θ)\pi\in\Delta(\Theta) and g∈ΛDg\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}. We have that

ℛ⁡(𝔓#​π,g)=𝔓#​(ℛ0​(π,g)):={𝔓#​ξ|ξ∈ℛ0​(π,g)}and𝒮⁡(𝔓#​π,g)=𝒮0​(π,g).\mathcal{R}(\mathfrak{P}_{\#}\pi,g)=\mathfrak{P}_{\#}(\mathcal{R}_{0}(\pi,g)):=\left\{\mathfrak{P}_{\#}\xi\penalty\ \big|\penalty\ \xi\in\mathcal{R}_{0}(\pi,g)\right\}\penalty\ \penalty\ \text{and}\penalty\ \penalty\ \mathcal{S}(\mathfrak{P}_{\#}\pi,g)=\mathcal{S}_{0}(\pi,g).

Therefore, with a slight abuse of notation, given π∈Δ⁡(Θ)\pi\in\Delta(\Theta) and g∈ΛDg\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}, we denote the set ℛ0​(π,g)\mathcal{R}_{0}(\pi,g) by ℛ⁡(π,g)\mathcal{R}(\pi,g) and the set 𝒮0​(π,g)\mathcal{S}_{0}(\pi,g) by 𝒮⁡(π,g)\mathcal{S}(\pi,g), in order to maintain consistency with the notation used thus far. For π∈Δ⁡(Θ)\pi\in\Delta(\Theta), we likewise write L1​(π):=L1​(𝔓#​π)L^{1}(\pi):=L^{1}(\mathfrak{P}_{\#}\pi).

6.2 Convergence result

Given g∈ΛD∗g\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}^{*} and π∈Δ⁡(Θ)\pi\in\Delta(\Theta), in the following algorithms, we will need to numerically approximate the decision functional

∫Θ𝔼μθ​[X]​g∘π⁡(𝑑θ)=supμ∈𝒮⁡(π,g)𝔼μ​[X],X∈L1​(π).\int_{\Theta}\mathbb{E}^{\mu_{\theta}}[X]g\circ\pi(\mathrm{d}\theta)=\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal{S}(\pi,g)}\mathbb{E}^{\mu}[X],\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in L^{1}(\pi).

Many of the numerical schemes found in the literature can produce a stochastic process (θn)n∈ℕ(\theta_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} with values in the parameter space Θ\Theta such that

limn→∞1n​∑k=1nf⁡(θk)=∫Θf​𝑑πκ​-a.s.,\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}f(\theta_{k})=\int_{\Theta}f\mathrm{d}\pi\penalty\ \penalty\ \kappa\text{-a.s.}, (8)

where f:Θ→ℝf:\Theta\to\mathbb{R} is measurable and satisfies ∫Θ|f|​𝑑π<∞\int_{\Theta}|f|\mathrm{d}\pi<\infty, and κ∈Δ⁡(Θℕ)\kappa\in\Delta(\Theta^{\mathbb{N}}) is the probability measure induced by the stochastic process on path space. For example, many of the schemes used to sample from the posterior probability measure in Bayesian statistics satisfy this property; see Meyn and Tweedie (2012). Additionally, if we are able to sample π\pi directly, we may take κ=πℕ\kappa=\pi^{\mathbb{N}}, in which case, (8) follows directly from the law of large numbers. For the numerical examples in the following subsection, we assume that π\pi can be sampled directly. Nevertheless, we formulate the next theorem under the more general condition (8) in order to motivate the use of MCMC-type algorithms in settings where direct sampling from π\pi is not available.

Theorem 7.

Given a stochastic process (θn)n∈ℕ(\theta_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} satisfying (8), π∈Δ⁡(Θ)\pi\in\Delta(\Theta), X∈L1​(π)X\in L^{1}(\pi), and g∈ΛD∗g\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}^{*}, define Yn=𝔼μθn​[X]Y_{n}=\mathbb{E}^{\mu_{\theta_{n}}}[X]. We have that

limn→∞∑k=1n(g(n−k+1n)−g(n−kn))Yk:n=∫Θ𝔼μθ[X]g∘π(dθ),κ-a.s.,\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(g\left(\frac{n-k+1}{n}\right)-g\left(\frac{n-k}{n}\right)\right)Y_{k:n}=\int_{\Theta}\mathbb{E}^{\mu_{\theta}}[X]g\circ\pi(\mathrm{d}\theta),\penalty\ \penalty\ \kappa\text{-a.s.,}

where Yk:nY_{k:n} denotes the kkth order statistic of the random vector (Y1,…,Yn)(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n}).

6.3 Numerical illustrations

In this section, we numerically implement the alternative formulas for (5) derived in Section 4, using Theorem 7 to approximate the associated Choquet integrals. A portfolio optimization example illustrates how ambiguity perception and ambiguity attitude affect the resulting evaluations.

In all numerical implementations, we assume that (Ω,ℱ)=(ℝ2,ℬ⁡(ℝ2))(\Omega,\mathcal{F})=(\mathbb{R}^{2},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{2})). The parameter space is taken to be Θ=ℝ2×(0,∞)2×(−1,1),\Theta=\mathbb{R}^{2}\times(0,\infty)^{2}\times(-1,1), with the parametrization

Θ∋(m1,m2,σ1,σ2,c)↦MVN2​((m1m2),(σ12c​σ1​σ2c​σ1​σ2σ22)).\Theta\ni(m_{1},m_{2},\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},c)\mapsto\mathrm{MVN}_{2}\left(\begin{pmatrix}m_{1}\\ m_{2}\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{1}^{2}&c\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\\ c\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}&\sigma_{2}^{2}\end{pmatrix}\right).

Let X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} denote the acts given by the marginal projections, representing the single-period percentage losses of two financial positions. Our objective is to evaluate

supν∈𝒮⁡(π,gβ)γ⁡(w​X1+(1−w)​X2|ν),\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{S}(\pi,g_{\beta})}\gamma(wX_{1}+(1-w)X_{2}|\nu), (9)

where γ:𝒟1→ℝ∪{∞}\gamma:\mathcal{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\} is a statistic, w∈[0,1]w\in[0,1], β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1), and gβ​(x)=x1−β∧1g_{\beta}(x)=\frac{x}{1-\beta}\wedge 1 for all x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1]. Since gβ≥gβ′⇔β≥β′g_{\beta}\geq g_{\beta^{\prime}}\iff\beta\geq\beta^{\prime}, the parameter β\beta corresponds to ambiguity aversion attitudes, with larger values of β\beta corresponding to greater ambiguity aversion. Finally, in each numerical implementation, we consider the three second-order models listed in Table 1, specifying the marginal distributions, as we assume the components are independent.

Note that the distributions of the acts X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} under the predictive model are the same for both π1\pi_{1} and π2\pi_{2} in Table 1. Additionally, under π1\pi_{1}, we perceive no ambiguity for the act X1X_{1}, as defined in Section 5. Therefore, in the numerical implementations later, the decision functional in (9) should assign the same value to X1X_{1} (w=1w=1) and X2X_{2} (w=0w=0) under ambiguity neutrality (β=0\beta=0). However, as we become more ambiguity averse (β\beta increases), the decision functional should assign a higher value to X2X_{2} (w=0w=0) than to X1X_{1} (w=1w=1).

Expected shortfall.

Figure 3 presents the values of the decision functional (9) when γ=ES0.95\gamma=\mathrm{ES}_{0.95}. Under the second-order model π1\pi_{1} (left panel), the ambiguity-neutral case (β=0\beta=0) is minimized by an equal allocation between X1X_{1} and X2X_{2}. This is consistent with the preference for equal diversification, since X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} have the same distribution under the predictive model. As β\beta increases, however, the minimizing portfolio shifts monotonically toward a full allocation in X1X_{1}. This is consistent with interpreting β\beta as a parameter of ambiguity aversion: under π1\pi_{1}, ambiguity is perceived in the distribution of X2X_{2}, but ambiguity is not perceived in the distribution of X1X_{1}.

This story changes in the center and right panels, corresponding to the second-order models π2\pi_{2} and π3\pi_{3}, respectively. In both cases, ambiguity is perceived in the distributions of X1X_{1} and X2X_{2}. For π2\pi_{2}, increasing β\beta produces little deviation from the fact that an equal allocation between X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} minimizes the decision functional. This is because the ambiguity associated with the two assets is roughly comparable. The case of π3\pi_{3} differs markedly. There, the predictive distribution of X2X_{2} is roughly as favorable as that of X1X_{1}, but π3\pi_{3} perceives greater ambiguity in X2X_{2} than in X1X_{1} (e.g., the standard deviation of X2X_{2} is ambiguous). As a result, when ambiguity aversion increases, the minimizer shifts toward a larger allocation in X1X_{1}.

Monotone mean–variance.

To further illustrate the scope of Theorem 4, we consider the monotone mean–variance statistic from Maccheroni et al. (2009). This statistic is the optimized certainty equivalent generated by

hζ​(x)=ζ​(x+12​ζ)+2−14​ζ,x∈ℝ,h_{\zeta}(x)=\zeta\left(x+\frac{1}{2\zeta}\right)_{+}^{2}-\frac{1}{4\zeta},\penalty\ \penalty\ x\in\mathbb{R},

where ζ∈(0,∞)\zeta\in(0,\infty) is a risk aversion parameter. It provides a monotone counterpart to the classical mean–variance criterion from Markowitz (1952) while retaining its quadratic sensitivity to losses.

Figure 4 plots the negative worst-case functional for ζ=2\zeta=2. We plot the negative of the worst-case monotone mean–variance functional so that it is expressed in utility terms: maximizing this quantity is equivalent to minimizing worst-case risk and mimics the familiar maxmin utility formulation. As ambiguity aversion increases, the utility curves shift downward. The accompanying movement of the maximizing portfolio toward X1X_{1}, particularly under π1\pi_{1} and π3\pi_{3}, shows that ambiguity aversion can materially alter the optimal allocation.

Entropic risk measure.

Figure 5 in Appendix H presents the values of the decision functional (9) when γ=ER10\gamma=\mathrm{ER}_{10}. An interesting contrast between the numerical results in Figure 3 and those in Figure 5 arises under the second-order model π3\pi_{3} (right panel). For low values of β\beta, the minimizing portfolio fully allocates to X2X_{2}. As β\beta increases, however, the minimizing portfolio shifts toward X1X_{1}. Intuitively, this happens since the standard deviation of X2X_{2} is ambiguous. This differs from the previous results because ER10\mathrm{ER}_{10} evaluated on the predictive distribution of X2X_{2} is much smaller than when evaluated on the predictive distribution of X1X_{1}.

Value-at-risk.

Figure 6 in Appendix H reports the worst-case value-at-risk at level α=0.95\alpha=0.95. At β=0\beta=0, the criterion reduces to value-at-risk under the predictive model. Under π1\pi_{1}, increasing β\beta shifts the minimizing portfolio toward X1X_{1}, and all curves coincide at w=1w=1 because the distribution of X1X_{1} is unambiguous. The movement is more modest under π2\pi_{2}, where the ambiguity associated with the two assets is more comparable, while under π3\pi_{3} the ambiguity in the mean and standard deviation of X2X_{2} again shifts the minimizing allocation toward X1X_{1}.

7 Consistency and model misspecification

The preceding section studies whether posterior concentration leads the decision functional to recover the chosen statistic under the data-generating model. Under the stated continuity conditions, this holds when the posterior concentrates on the correct parameter. Under misspecification, however, posterior concentration can leave persistent model error. We therefore study a robustification of the statistic that accounts for misspecification separately from ambiguity perception and ambiguity attitude.

We will assume that the parametrization 𝔓\mathfrak{P} is continuous with respect to the total variation metric on Δ\Delta, where

dTV​(μ,μ~)=supA∈ℱ|μ⁡(A)−μ~​(A)|,(μ,μ~)∈Δ2.d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,\tilde{\mu})=\sup_{A\in\mathcal{F}}|\mu(A)-\tilde{\mu}(A)|,\penalty\ \penalty\ (\mu,\tilde{\mu})\in\Delta^{2}.

This implies that the parametrization is continuous with respect to the weak topology τ\tau. This assumption is reasonable, as many regular parametric models satisfy it.

In this section, statistics will have domain ℰ=𝒟c\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{D}_{c} and decision functionals will have domain 𝒴=𝒳b\mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{X}_{b}. A collection 𝒬⊆𝒟c\mathcal{Q}\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{c} is said to have uniformly bounded support if there exists a compact set that contains the support of each Q∈𝒬Q\in\mathcal{Q}. We say that a statistic γ\gamma is Lebesgue continuous if for all sequences (Qn)n∈ℕ⊆𝒟c(Q_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{c} with uniformly bounded support satisfying Qn⇒QQ_{n}\Rightarrow Q for some Q∈𝒟cQ\in\mathcal{D}_{c}, we have that limn→∞γ⁡(Qn)=γ⁡(Q)\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma(Q_{n})=\gamma(Q).

7.1 Bayesian consistency

In Bayesian statistics, consistency concerns the asymptotic behavior of the posterior distribution (second-order model). For example, suppose we observe an IID sequence of random variables (ζk)k∈ℕ(\zeta_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} taking values in Ω\Omega. Assume that ζk∼μθ0\zeta_{k}\sim\mu_{\theta_{0}} for some θ0∈Θ\theta_{0}\in\Theta. Under certain regularity conditions, see Ghosal and van der Vaart (2017), we have that the sequence of second-order models (πn)n∈ℕ(\pi_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} given by the posterior distribution (πn\pi_{n} is obtained after realizing (ζk)k=1n(\zeta_{k})_{k=1}^{n}) satisfies

πn⇒δθ0μθ0∞​-a.s.\pi_{n}\Rightarrow\delta_{\theta_{0}}\penalty\ \penalty\ \mu_{\theta_{0}}^{\infty}\text{-a.s.}

The following theorem verifies that the decision functional (5), under the distortion ambiguity iron, asymptotically agrees with the correct value.

Theorem 8.

Let (πn)n∈ℕ⊆Δ⁡(Θ)(\pi_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\Delta(\Theta) be a sequence such that πn⇒δθ0\pi_{n}\Rightarrow\delta_{\theta_{0}} for some θ0∈Θ\theta_{0}\in\Theta. Let g∈ΛDg\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}} and γ\gamma be a Lebesgue continuous statistic. Then, we have that

limn→∞maxν∈𝒮⁡(πn,g)⁡γ⁡(X|ν)=γ⁡(X|μθ0),X∈𝒳b.\lim_{n\to\infty}\max_{\nu\in\mathcal{S}(\pi_{n},g)}\gamma(X|\nu)=\gamma(X|\mu_{\theta_{0}}),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}.

Finally, we have a result regarding the actual ambiguity sets. This result shows that, asymptotically, the first-order models in the ambiguity set are arbitrarily close to the true model.

Proposition 9.

Let (πn)n∈ℕ⊆Δ⁡(Θ)(\pi_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\Delta(\Theta) be a sequence such that πn⇒δθ0\pi_{n}\Rightarrow\delta_{\theta_{0}} for some θ0∈Θ\theta_{0}\in\Theta and g∈ΛDg\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}. Then, we have that

limn→∞supν∈𝒮⁡(πn,g)dTV​(ν,μθ0)=0.\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{S}(\pi_{n},g)}d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\nu,\mu_{\theta_{0}})=0.

The next subsection discusses how concerns regarding model misspecification can be incorporated into these decision functionals.

7.2 Model misspecification

Model misspecification refers to the case in which the parametric model (Θ,𝔓)(\Theta,\mathfrak{P}) fails to contain the true first-order model that generates the random phenomenon. In the Bayesian literature, there are results on the asymptotic behavior of the posterior distribution (second-order model). For example, as in the preceding subsection, suppose we observe an IID sequence of random variables (ζk)k∈ℕ(\zeta_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} taking values in Ω\Omega. We now consider the misspecified case, meaning that ζk∼μ0\zeta_{k}\sim\mu_{0}, but, unlike the preceding subsection, no parameter θ0∈Θ\theta_{0}\in\Theta satisfies μ0=μθ0\mu_{0}=\mu_{\theta_{0}}. However, assume that the mapping

Θ→ℝ∪{∞}:θ↦KL⁡(μ0|μθ),\Theta\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}:\theta\mapsto\mathrm{KL}(\mu_{0}|\mu_{\theta}),

admits a unique minimizer. We denote this minimizer by θ0\theta_{0}. Under certain regularity conditions, see Berk (1966), we have that the sequence of second-order models (πn)n∈ℕ(\pi_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} given by the posterior distribution (πn\pi_{n} is obtained after realizing (ζk)k=1n(\zeta_{k})_{k=1}^{n}) satisfies

πn⇒δθ0μ0∞​-a.s.\pi_{n}\Rightarrow\delta_{\theta_{0}}\penalty\ \penalty\ \mu_{0}^{\infty}\text{-a.s.}

Therefore, a natural way for a DM to address model misspecification is to first robustify their statistic. The following proposition discusses how this can be done.

Proposition 10.

Given a statistic γ\gamma, atomless μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta, and ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists a statistic γϵKL\gamma_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{KL}} satisfying

γϵKL​(X|μ)=supν∈KL⁡(μ,ϵ)γ⁡(X|ν),X∈𝒳b,\gamma_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{KL}}(X|\mu)=\sup_{\nu\in\mathrm{KL}(\mu;\epsilon)}\gamma(X|\nu),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b},

where KL⁡(μ,ϵ)={ν∈Δ|KL⁡(ν|μ)≤ϵ}\mathrm{KL}(\mu;\epsilon)=\{\nu\in\Delta\penalty\ |\penalty\ \mathrm{KL}(\nu|\mu)\leq\epsilon\}. Moreover, if γ\gamma is Lebesgue continuous, then γϵKL\gamma_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{KL}} is Lebesgue continuous.

Example 5.

Given ϵ>0\epsilon>0, the statistic 𝔼ϵKL\mathbb{E}^{\mathrm{KL}}_{\epsilon} is known as entropic value-at-risk; see Föllmer and Knispel (2011) and Ahmadi-Javid (2012).

Assuming the DM uses γ\gamma to represent their pure-risk preferences, if they were worried about model misspecification, given π∈Δ⁡(Θ)\pi\in\Delta(\Theta), g∈ΛDg\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{D}}, and ϵ>0\epsilon>0, they could define the decision functional

ρ⁡(X,π,g,ϵ)=supν∈𝒮⁡(π,g)γϵKL​(X|ν),X∈𝒳b.\rho(X;\pi,g,\epsilon)=\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{S}(\pi,g)}\gamma^{\mathrm{KL}}_{\epsilon}(X|\nu),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}. (10)

The parameter ϵ\epsilon in (10) represents the DM’s fear of model misspecification. For example, if it holds that ϵ≥KL⁡(μ0|μθ0)\epsilon\geq\mathrm{KL}(\mu_{0}|\mu_{\theta_{0}}) and γ\gamma is Lebesgue continuous, then, by Theorem 8, we have

limn→∞ρ⁡(X,πn,g,ϵ)=γϵKL​(X|μθ0)≥γ⁡(X|μ0),X∈𝒳b.\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho(X;\pi_{n},g,\epsilon)=\gamma_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{KL}}(X|\mu_{\theta_{0}})\geq\gamma(X|\mu_{0}),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}. (11)

Therefore, the DM does not asymptotically underestimate the true value of their statistic under model misspecification.

Independently of the asymptotic result, the decision functional in (10) is interesting from a conceptual point of view. This follows because the decision functional separates the perception of ambiguity (π\pi), the attitude toward ambiguity (gg), and the attitude toward model misspecification (ϵ\epsilon). The joint incorporation of attitudes toward ambiguity and model misspecification into decision functionals was discussed in Cerreia-Vioglio et al. (2026).

In Shapiro et al. (2023), the authors also study decision functionals in a Bayesian context that address model misspecification. In that work, given π∈Δ⁡(Θ)\pi\in\Delta(\Theta) and ϵ>0\epsilon>0, the authors define the decision functional

ρ⁡(X,π,ϵ)=∫Θ𝔼ϵKL​(X|μθ)​π​(𝑑θ),X∈𝒳b.\rho(X;\pi,\epsilon)=\int_{\Theta}\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{KL}}(X|\mu_{\theta})\pi(\mathrm{d}\theta),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}. (12)

One can show that for all X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, a consistency result analogous to (11) holds for the decision functional in (12). However, the decision functional (12) has no mechanism to account for attitudes toward ambiguity. Moreover, we have the following proposition. We verify in Appendix G that, given X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, 𝔼ϵKL∘ιX\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{KL}}\circ\iota_{X} is Σ\Sigma-measurable.

Proposition 11.

If π~,π∈Π\tilde{\pi},\pi\in\Pi satisfy π~≥cxπ\tilde{\pi}\geq_{\mathrm{cx}}\pi, then

∫Δ𝔼ϵKL​(X|ν)​π~​(𝑑ν)≤∫Δ𝔼ϵKL​(X|ν)​π​(𝑑ν),X∈𝒳b\int_{\Delta}\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{KL}}(X|\nu)\tilde{\pi}(\mathrm{d}\nu)\leq\int_{\Delta}\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{KL}}(X|\nu)\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}

Therefore, the decision functional in (12) reflects an ambiguity-seeking attitude, as discussed in Section 3. Although the decision functionals in (10) and (12) exhibit a similar asymptotic property, they can lead to substantially different decisions in finite samples.

8 Conclusion

Bayesian second-order beliefs can be incorporated into decision functionals without changing the statistic governing pure-risk preferences. The difficulty is that averaging model-specific evaluations need not preserve ambiguity neutrality or strong ambiguity aversion. Ambiguity irons address this difficulty by translating a second-order model and an ambiguity attitude into an ambiguity set, over which the original statistic is evaluated in the worst case. This construction gives Bayesian beliefs and distributionally robust optimization complementary roles in the same decision model.

The distortion ambiguity iron provides a concrete implementation of this approach. It produces convex, compact ambiguity sets and reduces evaluation to the prescribed statistic for acts with an unambiguous distribution. Alternative representations support numerical implementation, and an order-statistic approximation gives pointwise convergence for the underlying Choquet integrals. Portfolio examples illustrate how ambiguity perception and attitude affect evaluations and allocations. When the posterior concentrates on the data-generating model, the stated continuity conditions ensure that ambiguity sets contract and decision functionals recover their pure-risk values.

Posterior concentration does not eliminate misspecification when the model family excludes the data-generating distribution. The proposed KL-based robustification keeps this concern distinct from ambiguity within the model family. Further work may examine alternative ambiguity irons, convergence of optimal decisions, and dynamic decision problems with posterior updating.

Appendices: Omitted proofs and additional results

Appendix A Additional results needed for the proofs

Given n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, denote by 𝒳n\mathcal{X}_{n} the set of all X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b} such that n≥X≥−nn\geq X\geq-n. Additionally, denote by 𝒞n\mathcal{C}_{n} the set of all X∈𝒞bX\in\mathcal{C}_{b} such that n≥X≥−nn\geq X\geq-n.

Lemma 1.

Given n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and 𝒴⊆𝒳n\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathcal{X}_{n}, if 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is closed under pointwise convergence and 𝒞n⊆𝒴\mathcal{C}_{n}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}, then 𝒴=𝒳n\mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{X}_{n}.

Proof.

Define 𝒴0={X∈𝒳:(X∧n)∨(−n)∈𝒴}.\mathcal{Y}_{0}=\{X\in\mathcal{X}:(X\wedge n)\vee(-n)\in\mathcal{Y}\}. Since 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is closed under pointwise convergence, 𝒴0\mathcal{Y}_{0} is closed under pointwise convergence. Since 𝒞n⊆𝒴\mathcal{C}_{n}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}, 𝒞⊆𝒴0\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}_{0}. Therefore, by Kechris (2012, Theorem 11.6), 𝒴0=𝒳\mathcal{Y}_{0}=\mathcal{X}. Therefore, 𝒴=𝒳n\mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{X}_{n}. ∎

Denote by τb\tau_{b} the coarsest topology on Δ\Delta where the maps {ψX}X∈𝒳b\{\psi_{X}\}_{X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}} are continuous.

Proposition 12.

Let γ\gamma be a Lebesgue continuous statistic. Given X∈𝒞bX\in\mathcal{C}_{b}, γ∘ιX\gamma\circ\iota_{X} is τ\tau-continuous. Given X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, γ∘ιX\gamma\circ\iota_{X} is τb\tau_{b}-continuous.

Proof.

Given a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R} satisfying a≤ba\leq b, denote the set of Borel probability measures on ℝ\mathbb{R} with support contained in the interval [a,b][a,b] by 𝒟[a,b]\mathcal{D}_{[a,b]}. Denote by τ𝒟[a,b]\tau_{\mathcal{D}_{[a,b]}} the subspace topology on 𝒟[a,b]\mathcal{D}_{[a,b]} from the topology τ𝒟\tau_{\mathcal{D}}. As γ\gamma is Lebesgue continuous, γ|𝒟[a,b]\gamma|_{\mathcal{D}_{[a,b]}} is τ𝒟[a,b]\tau_{\mathcal{D}_{[a,b]}}-continuous.

Let X∈𝒞bX\in\mathcal{C}_{b}. We claim that ιX\iota_{X} is τ/τ𝒟\tau/\tau_{\mathcal{D}}-continuous. To see this, let (μk)k∈ℕ⊆Δ(\mu_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\Delta be a sequence such that μk⇒μ\mu_{k}\Rightarrow\mu for some μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta. Let f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be bounded and continuous. We have

limk→∞∫ℝf​d​ιX​(μk)=limk→∞𝔼μk​[f⁡(X)]=𝔼μ​[f⁡(X)]=∫ℝf​d​ιX​(μ).\lim_{k\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}}f\mathrm{d}\iota_{X}(\mu_{k})=\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathbb{E}^{\mu_{k}}[f(X)]=\mathbb{E}^{\mu}[f(X)]=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f\mathrm{d}\iota_{X}(\mu).

Therefore, ιX​(μk)⇒ιX​(μ)\iota_{X}(\mu_{k})\Rightarrow\iota_{X}(\mu), and ιX\iota_{X} is τ/τ𝒟\tau/\tau_{\mathcal{D}}-continuous. Since ιX​(Δ)⊆𝒟[a,b]\iota_{X}(\Delta)\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{[a,b]}, where a≤X≤ba\leq X\leq b, we have that γ∘ιX\gamma\circ\iota_{X} is τ\tau-continuous. A similar argument will show that, for all X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, γ∘ιX\gamma\circ\iota_{X} is τb\tau_{b}-continuous. ∎

Proposition 13.

Let γ\gamma be a Lebesgue continuous statistic and X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}. The mapping γ∘ιX\gamma\circ\iota_{X} is Σ\Sigma-measurable.

Proof.

Fix n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and define

𝒴={X∈𝒳n|γ∘ιX​is​Σ​-measurable}.\mathcal{Y}=\left\{X\in\mathcal{X}_{n}\penalty\ |\penalty\ \gamma\circ\iota_{X}\penalty\ \text{is}\penalty\ \Sigma\text{-measurable}\right\}.

By Proposition 12, we have that 𝒞n⊆𝒴\mathcal{C}_{n}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}. Let (Xk)k∈ℕ⊆𝒴(X_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathcal{Y} converge pointwise to some X∈𝒳nX\in\mathcal{X}_{n}. Since γ\gamma is Lebesgue continuous, n≥Xk≥−nn\geq X_{k}\geq-n for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, and (Xk)#​ν⇒X#​ν(X_{k})_{\#}\nu\Rightarrow X_{\#}\nu for all ν∈Δ\nu\in\Delta, we have that

limk→∞γ∘ιXk​(ν)=limk→∞γ⁡(Xk|ν)=γ⁡(X|ν)=γ∘ιX​(ν),ν∈Δ.\lim_{k\to\infty}\gamma\circ\iota_{X_{k}}(\nu)=\lim_{k\to\infty}\gamma(X_{k}|\nu)=\gamma(X|\nu)=\gamma\circ\iota_{X}(\nu),\penalty\ \penalty\ \nu\in\Delta.

Since γ∘ιXk\gamma\circ\iota_{X_{k}} is Σ\Sigma-measurable for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, γ∘ιX\gamma\circ\iota_{X} is Σ\Sigma-measurable. By Lemma 1, we have that 𝒴=𝒳n\mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{X}_{n}. Since n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} was arbitrary, the proof is complete. ∎

Proposition 13 guarantees that the integrals in the following proposition are well-defined.

Corollary 1.

Given convex φ:ℝ→ℝ\varphi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} and π~,π∈Π\tilde{\pi},\pi\in\Pi satisfying π~≥cxπ\tilde{\pi}\geq_{\mathrm{cx}}\pi, we have

∫Δφ⁡(𝔼ν​[X])​π~​(𝑑ν)≥∫Δφ⁡(𝔼ν​[X])​π​(𝑑ν).\int_{\Delta}\varphi(\mathbb{E}^{\nu}[X])\tilde{\pi}(\mathrm{d}\nu)\geq\int_{\Delta}\varphi(\mathbb{E}^{\nu}[X])\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu).

∫Δℓ⁡(γ⁡(X|ν))​π0​(𝑑ν)=∫Ωℓ⁡(γ⁡(X|κ⁡(ω)))​μ​(𝑑ω)=∫Ωℓ⁡(γ⁡(δX⁡(ω)))​μ​(𝑑ω)=𝔼μ​[ℓ⁡(X)],X∈𝒳b.\int_{\Delta}\ell(\gamma(X|\nu))\pi_{0}(\mathrm{d}\nu)=\int_{\Omega}\ell(\gamma(X|\kappa(\omega)))\mu(\mathrm{d}\omega)=\int_{\Omega}\ell\left(\gamma\left(\delta_{X(\omega)}\right)\right)\mu(\mathrm{d}\omega)=\mathbb{E}^{\mu}[\ell(X)],\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}.

𝔼ℓ​(X|μ)=ℓ−1​(𝔼μ​[ℓ⁡(X)])=ℓ−1​(∫Δℓ⁡(γ⁡(X|ν))​π0​(𝑑ν))=γ⁡(X|ℜ⁡(π0)),X∈𝒳b.\mathbb{E}_{\ell}(X|\mu)=\ell^{-1}\left(\mathbb{E}^{\mu}[\ell(X)]\right)=\ell^{-1}\left(\int_{\Delta}\ell(\gamma(X|\nu))\pi_{0}(\mathrm{d}\nu)\right)=\gamma(X|\mathfrak{R}(\pi_{0})),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}.

Since μ\mu and ℜ⁡(π0)\mathfrak{R}(\pi_{0}) are both atomless, by Liebrich (2024, Proposition 2 and Theorem 6), ℜ⁡(π0)=μ\mathfrak{R}(\pi_{0})=\mu. Therefore, 𝔼ℓ​(X|μ)=γ⁡(X|μ)\mathbb{E}_{\ell}(X|\mu)=\gamma(X|\mu) for all X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}. Since μ\mu is atomless, we have that γ​(Q)=𝔼ℓ​(Q)\gamma(Q)=\mathbb{E}_{\ell}(Q) for all Q∈𝒟cQ\in\mathcal{D}_{c}. Thus, γ=𝔼ℓ\gamma=\mathbb{E}_{\ell}.

Finally, for all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, by assumption, we have that

𝔼ℓ​(X|μπ)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\ell}(X|\mu_{\pi}) =ℓ−1​(∫Δℓ⁡(𝔼ℓ​(X|ν))​π​(𝑑ν))\displaystyle=\ell^{-1}\left(\int_{\Delta}\ell(\mathbb{E}_{\ell}(X|\nu))\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)\right)
=ℓ−1​(∫Δℓ⁡(γ⁡(X|ν))​π​(𝑑ν))=γ⁡(X|ℜ⁡(π))=𝔼ℓ​(X|ℜ⁡(π)),X∈𝒳b.\displaystyle=\ell^{-1}\left(\int_{\Delta}\ell(\gamma(X|\nu))\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu)\right)=\gamma(X|\mathfrak{R}(\pi))=\mathbb{E}_{\ell}(X|\mathfrak{R}(\pi)),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}.

Therefore, for all A∈ℱA\in\mathcal{F}, we have that

ℓ−1​(μπ​(A))=𝔼ℓ​(𝟙A|μπ)=𝔼ℓ​(𝟙A|ℜ⁡(π))=ℓ−1​([ℜ⁡(π)]​(A)),\ell^{-1}(\mu_{\pi}(A))=\mathbb{E}_{\ell}(\mathds{1}_{A}|\mu_{\pi})=\mathbb{E}_{\ell}(\mathds{1}_{A}|\mathfrak{R}(\pi))=\ell^{-1}(\left[\mathfrak{R}(\pi)\right](A)),

and ℜ⁡(π)=μπ\mathfrak{R}(\pi)=\mu_{\pi}. Since π\pi was arbitrary, the proof is complete.

Conversely, if γ=𝔼ℓ\gamma=\mathbb{E}_{\ell} and ℜ⁡(π)=μπ\mathfrak{R}(\pi)=\mu_{\pi} for every π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, then (4) follows immediately from (1). ∎

Verification 3.

For all X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, the mapping ESα∘ιX\mathrm{ES}_{\alpha}\circ\iota_{X} is Σ\Sigma-measurable.

Proof.

Since ESα\mathrm{ES}_{\alpha} is Lebesgue continuous, by Proposition 13, ESα∘ιX\mathrm{ES}_{\alpha}\circ\iota_{X} is Σ\Sigma-measurable for X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}. ∎

Let X∈𝒞bX\in\mathcal{C}_{b}. As ESα\mathrm{ES}_{\alpha} is Lebesgue continuous, by Proposition 12, ESα∘ιX\mathrm{ES}_{\alpha}\circ\iota_{X} is τ\tau-continuous. limβ∫Δf​d​ξφ⁡(β)=∫Δf​𝑑ξ\lim_{\beta}\int_{\Delta}f\mathrm{d}\xi_{\varphi(\beta)}=\int_{\Delta}f\mathrm{d}\xi

Therefore, μφ⁡(β)→μ\mu_{\varphi(\beta)}\to\mu in τb\tau_{b}. Verification 4.

The mapping ν↦KL⁡(μ|ν)\nu\mapsto\mathrm{KL}(\mu|\nu) is Σ\Sigma-measurable for all μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta.

Proof.

Since (Ω,ℱ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F}) is a Polish measurable space, by Donsker and Varadhan (1983, Equation (2.1)), we know that for all μ,ν∈Δ\mu,\nu\in\Delta,

KL⁡(μ|ν)=supX∈𝒞b(𝔼μ​[X]−log⁡(𝔼ν​[eX])).\mathrm{KL}(\mu|\nu)=\sup_{X\in\mathcal{C}_{b}}\left(\mathbb{E}^{\mu}[X]-\log\left(\mathbb{E}^{\nu}\left[e^{X}\right]\right)\right).

Given μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta and X∈𝒞bX\in\mathcal{C}_{b}, since the mapping

is τ\tau-continuous, the mapping ν↦KL⁡(μ|ν)\nu\mapsto\mathrm{KL}(\mu|\nu) is τ\tau-lower semicontinuous. Since τ\tau-lower semicontinuity implies Σ\Sigma-measurability, we have shown the original claim. ∎

For x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, define H⁡(x)=supν∈𝒮⁡(π,g)ν⁡(X>x).H(x)=\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{S}(\pi,g)}\nu(X>x). Applying (6) gives

limx→∞π(ν:ν(X>x)>t)=0.\lim_{x\to\infty}\pi(\nu:\nu(X>x)>t)=0.

Since gg is continuous, by the dominated convergence theorem, we have that limx→∞H⁡(x)=0\lim_{x\to\infty}H(x)=0.

ν⁡(X>b)≤H⁡(b)≤1−α,ν∈𝒮⁡(π,g).\nu(X>b)\leq H(b)\leq 1-\alpha,\penalty\ \penalty\ \nu\in\mathcal{S}(\pi,g).

x0=supν∈𝒮⁡(π,g)VaRα​(X|ν)∈ℝ.x_{0}=\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{S}(\pi,g)}\mathrm{VaR}_{\alpha}(X|\nu)\in\mathbb{R}.

ν⁡(X>x0+ϵ)≤1−α,ν∈𝒮⁡(π,g).\nu(X>x_{0}+\epsilon)\leq 1-\alpha,\penalty\ \penalty\ \nu\in\mathcal{S}(\pi,g).

Taking the supremum over ν\nu gives H⁡(x0+ϵ)≤1−αH(x_{0}+\epsilon)\leq 1-\alpha, so y0≤x0+ϵy_{0}\leq x_{0}+\epsilon. Letting ϵ↓0\epsilon\downarrow 0 yields y0≤x0y_{0}\leq x_{0}. ∎

Therefore, the proof is complete. ∎
