Proposition 10 is a corollary of Proposition 16 and Proposition 17, presented and proved below. Given μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta, we define Δ⁡(μ)={ν∈Δ|ν≪μ}\Delta(\mu)=\{\nu\in\Delta\penalty\ |\penalty\ \nu\ll\mu\}. Given μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta and X,Y∈𝒳X,Y\in\mathcal{X}, we say X​=dμ​YX\overset{\mathrm{d}}{=}_{\mu}Y if X#​μ=Y#​μX_{\#}\mu=Y_{\#}\mu. Given μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta, we say that the decision functional ρ:𝒳b→ℝ\rho:\mathcal{X}_{b}\to\mathbb{R} is μ\mu-law invariant if ρ⁡(X)=ρ⁡(Y)\rho(X)=\rho(Y) for all X,Y∈𝒳bX,Y\in\mathcal{X}_{b} satisfying X​=dμ​YX\overset{\mathrm{d}}{=}_{\mu}Y. Clearly, if μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta is atomless, a decision functional ρ\rho is μ\mu-law invariant if and only if there exists a statistic γ\gamma such that ρ⁡(X)=γ⁡(X|μ)\rho(X)=\gamma(X|\mu) for all X∈𝒳b.X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}. Given μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta and ν∈Δ⁡(μ)\nu\in\Delta(\mu), define

𝒯⁡(ν|μ)={ν~∈Δ⁡(μ)|d​ν~d​μ​=dμ​d​νd​μ}.\mathcal{T}(\nu|\mu)=\left\{\tilde{\nu}\in\Delta(\mu)\penalty\ \bigg|\penalty\ \frac{\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\overset{\mathrm{d}}{=}_{\mu}\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\}.

Given μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta and 𝒫⊆Δ⁡(μ)\mathcal{P}\subseteq\Delta(\mu), we say that 𝒫\mathcal{P} is μ\mu-law invariant if for all ν∈𝒫\nu\in\mathcal{P}, 𝒯⁡(ν|μ)⊆𝒫\mathcal{T}(\nu|\mu)\subseteq\mathcal{P}. Given μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta, we say that X,Y∈𝒳X,Y\in\mathcal{X} are μ\mu-comonotonic if there exists A∈ℱA\in\mathcal{F} with μ⁡(A)=1\mu(A)=1 such that

(X⁡(ω)−X⁡(ω~))​(Y⁡(ω)−Y⁡(ω~))≥0,ω,ω~∈A.(X(\omega)-X(\tilde{\omega}))(Y(\omega)-Y(\tilde{\omega}))\geq 0,\penalty\ \penalty\ \omega,\tilde{\omega}\in A.
Proposition 16.

Let μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta be atomless and 𝒫⊆Δ⁡(μ)\mathcal{P}\subseteq\Delta(\mu) be nonempty and μ\mu-law invariant. Then, for all statistics γ\gamma, the decision functional

ρ⁡(X)=supν∈𝒫γ⁡(X|ν),X∈𝒳b,\rho(X)=\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}\gamma(X|\nu),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b},

is μ\mu-law invariant.

Proof.

Given X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, define

𝒫⁡(X)={ν∈𝒫|d​νd​μ​ and ​X​ are μ-comonotonic}.\mathcal{P}(X)=\left\{\nu\in\mathcal{P}\penalty\ \bigg|\penalty\ \frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\text{ and }X\text{ are $\mu$-comonotonic}\right\}.

Since 𝒫\mathcal{P} is μ\mu-law invariant, 𝒯⁡(ν|μ)⊆𝒫\mathcal{T}(\nu|\mu)\subseteq\mathcal{P} for all ν∈𝒫\nu\in\mathcal{P}. Additionally, since μ\mu is atomless, given ν∈𝒫\nu\in\mathcal{P} and X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, we have that 𝒯⁡(ν|μ)∩𝒫⁡(X)≠∅\mathcal{T}(\nu|\mu)\cap\mathcal{P}(X)\neq\varnothing; see Föllmer and Schied (2016, Lemma A.25). Let ν∈𝒫\nu\in\mathcal{P}, X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, and ν~∈𝒯⁡(ν|μ)∩𝒫⁡(X)\tilde{\nu}\in\mathcal{T}(\nu|\mu)\cap\mathcal{P}(X). By the Hardy–Littlewood inequality, we have that

ν⁡(X>x)=𝔼μ​[d​νd​μ​𝟙(x,∞)​(X)]≤𝔼μ​[d​ν~d​μ​𝟙(x,∞)​(X)]=ν~​(X>x),x∈ℝ.\nu(X>x)=\mathbb{E}^{\mu}\left[\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\mathds{1}_{(x,\infty)}(X)\right]\leq\mathbb{E}^{\mu}\left[\frac{\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\mathds{1}_{(x,\infty)}(X)\right]=\tilde{\nu}(X>x),\penalty\ \penalty\ x\in\mathbb{R}.

Thus, X#ν≤stX#ν~X_{\#}\nu\leq_{\mathrm{st}}X_{\#}\tilde{\nu} and γ⁡(X|ν)≤γ⁡(X|ν~)\gamma(X|\nu)\leq\gamma(X|\tilde{\nu}). Therefore, we have

ρ⁡(X)=supν∈𝒫γ⁡(X|ν)=supν∈𝒫supν~∈𝒯⁡(ν|μ)γ⁡(X|ν~)=supν∈𝒫supν~∈𝒯⁡(ν|μ)∩𝒫⁡(X)γ⁡(X|ν~)=supν∈𝒫⁡(X)γ⁡(X|ν),X∈𝒳b.\displaystyle\rho(X)=\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}\gamma(X|\nu)=\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}\sup_{\tilde{\nu}\in\mathcal{T}(\nu|\mu)}\gamma(X|\tilde{\nu})=\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}\sup_{\tilde{\nu}\in\mathcal{T}(\nu|\mu)\cap\mathcal{P}(X)}\gamma(X|\tilde{\nu})=\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}(X)}\gamma(X|\nu),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}.

Let X,Y∈𝒳bX,Y\in\mathcal{X}_{b} satisfy X​=dμ​YX\overset{\mathrm{d}}{=}_{\mu}Y. Let ν∈𝒫⁡(X)\nu\in\mathcal{P}(X) and ν~∈𝒯⁡(ν|μ)∩𝒫⁡(Y)\tilde{\nu}\in\mathcal{T}(\nu|\mu)\cap\mathcal{P}(Y). Since (X,d​νd​μ)​=dμ​(Y,d​ν~d​μ)\left(X,\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right)\overset{\mathrm{d}}{=}_{\mu}\left(Y,\frac{\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right), we have that

ν⁡(X>x)=𝔼μ​[d​νd​μ​𝟙(x,∞)​(X)]=𝔼μ​[d​ν~d​μ​𝟙(x,∞)​(Y)]=ν~​(Y>x),x∈ℝ.\nu(X>x)=\mathbb{E}^{\mu}\left[\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\mathds{1}_{(x,\infty)}(X)\right]=\mathbb{E}^{\mu}\left[\frac{\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\mathds{1}_{(x,\infty)}(Y)\right]=\tilde{\nu}(Y>x),\penalty\ \penalty\ x\in\mathbb{R}.

Thus, X#ν=stY#ν~X_{\#}\nu=_{\mathrm{st}}Y_{\#}\tilde{\nu} and γ⁡(X|ν)=γ⁡(Y|ν~)\gamma(X|\nu)=\gamma(Y|\tilde{\nu}). Since ν∈𝒫⁡(X)\nu\in\mathcal{P}(X) was arbitrary,

ρ⁡(X)=supν∈𝒫⁡(X)γ⁡(X|ν)≤supν∈𝒫⁡(Y)γ⁡(Y|ν)=ρ⁡(Y).\rho(X)=\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}(X)}\gamma(X|\nu)\leq\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}(Y)}\gamma(Y|\nu)=\rho(Y).

A similar argument will show that ρ⁡(Y)≤ρ⁡(X)\rho(Y)\leq\rho(X). Therefore, ρ⁡(X)=ρ⁡(Y)\rho(X)=\rho(Y) and ρ\rho is μ\mu-law invariant. ∎

We say that the decision functional ρ:𝒳b→ℝ\rho:\mathcal{X}_{b}\to\mathbb{R} is Lebesgue continuous if for bounded sequences (Xn)n∈ℕ⊆𝒳b(X_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathcal{X}_{b} that converge pointwise to some X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, we have that limn→∞ρ⁡(Xn)=ρ⁡(X)\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho(X_{n})=\rho(X). Clearly, if μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta is atomless, then the decision functional ρ:𝒳b→ℝ\rho:\mathcal{X}_{b}\to\mathbb{R} defined by ρ⁡(X)=γ⁡(X|μ)\rho(X)=\gamma(X|\mu), for some statistic γ\gamma, is Lebesgue continuous if and only if γ\gamma is Lebesgue continuous.

Proposition 17.

Let 𝒫⊆Δ\mathcal{P}\subseteq\Delta be nonempty and τb\tau_{b}-compact and γ\gamma be a Lebesgue continuous statistic. Then the decision functional

ρ⁡(X)=supν∈𝒫γ⁡(X|ν),X∈𝒳b,\rho(X)=\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}\gamma(X|\nu),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b},

is Lebesgue continuous.

Proof.

It is well-known that ρ\rho is Lebesgue continuous if and only if for all uniformly bounded pointwise-increasing or pointwise-decreasing sequences (Xn)n∈ℕ⊆𝒳b(X_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathcal{X}_{b}, we have that limn→∞ρ⁡(Xn)=ρ⁡(limn→∞Xn)\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho(X_{n})=\rho(\lim_{n\to\infty}X_{n}). Clearly, since γ\gamma is Lebesgue continuous, the above holds for all pointwise-increasing sequences. The hard part is showing that it is true for all pointwise-decreasing sequences. Therefore, let (Xn)n∈ℕ⊆𝒳b(X_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathcal{X}_{b} be a uniformly bounded pointwise-decreasing sequence and define X=limn→∞XnX=\lim_{n\to\infty}X_{n}.

Let ΦBL\Phi_{\mathrm{BL}} denote the set of all Lipschitz continuous functions f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} that are bounded by, and have Lipschitz constant less than, 1. It is well-known, see Dudley (2018, Theorem 11.3.3), that

dBL:𝒟2→[0,∞):(Q,P)↦supf∈ΦBL|∫ℝf⁡(x)​Q​(𝑑x)−∫ℝf⁡(x)​P​(𝑑x)|,d_{\mathrm{BL}}:\mathcal{D}^{2}\to[0,\infty):(Q,P)\mapsto\sup_{f\in\Phi_{\mathrm{BL}}}\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)Q(\mathrm{d}x)-\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)P(\mathrm{d}x)\right|,

is a metric and metrizes τ𝒟\tau_{\mathcal{D}}. We claim that

limn→∞supν∈𝒫dBL​((Xn)#​ν,X#​ν)=0.\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}d_{\mathrm{BL}}((X_{n})_{\#}\nu,X_{\#}\nu)=0.

Since 𝒫\mathcal{P} is τb\tau_{b}-compact, by Marinacci and Montrucchio (2004, Lemma 4.1) and Dunford and Schwartz (1988, Theorem IV.9.2), there exists μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta such that for all ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that

μ⁡(A)<δ⟹supν∈𝒫ν⁡(A)≤ϵ,A∈ℱ.\mu(A)<\delta\implies\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}\nu(A)\leq\epsilon,\penalty\ \penalty\ A\in\mathcal{F}.

Let ϵ>0\epsilon>0. By Egorov’s theorem, we can find A∈ℱA\in\mathcal{F} and N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} such that μ⁡(A)>1−δ\mu(A)>1-\delta and for all n≥Nn\geq N, we have |Xn​(ω)−X⁡(ω)|≤ϵ|X_{n}(\omega)-X(\omega)|\leq\epsilon for all ω∈A.\omega\in A. Therefore, since μ⁡(Ac)<δ\mu(A^{c})<\delta, for all n≥Nn\geq N,

supν∈𝒫dBL​((Xn)#​ν,X#​ν)\displaystyle\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}d_{\mathrm{BL}}((X_{n})_{\#}\nu,X_{\#}\nu) ≤supν∈𝒫supf∈ΦBL𝔼ν​[|f⁡(Xn)−f⁡(X)|]\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}\sup_{f\in\Phi_{\mathrm{BL}}}\mathbb{E}^{\nu}[\left|f(X_{n})-f(X)\right|]
≤supν∈𝒫supf∈ΦBL𝔼ν​[|f⁡(Xn)−f⁡(X)|​𝟙A]+supν∈𝒫supf∈ΦBL𝔼ν​[|f⁡(Xn)−f⁡(X)|​𝟙Ac]\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}\sup_{f\in\Phi_{\mathrm{BL}}}\mathbb{E}^{\nu}[\left|f(X_{n})-f(X)\right|\mathds{1}_{A}]+\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}\sup_{f\in\Phi_{\mathrm{BL}}}\mathbb{E}^{\nu}[\left|f(X_{n})-f(X)\right|\mathds{1}_{A^{c}}]
≤supν∈𝒫𝔼ν​[|Xn−X|​𝟙A]+2​supν∈𝒫ν⁡(Ac)≤3​ϵ.\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{E}^{\nu}[\left|X_{n}-X\right|\mathds{1}_{A}]+2\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}\nu(A^{c})\leq 3\epsilon.

Find a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R} such that a≤Xn≤ba\leq X_{n}\leq b for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. Let 𝒟[a,b]\mathcal{D}_{[a,b]} denote the set of Borel probability measures on ℝ\mathbb{R} with support contained in the interval [a,b][a,b]. Clearly, for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, (Xn)#​μ∈𝒟[a,b](X_{n})_{\#}\mu\in\mathcal{D}_{[a,b]} for all μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta. Additionally, X#​μ∈𝒟[a,b]X_{\#}\mu\in\mathcal{D}_{[a,b]} for all μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta. By Prokhorov’s theorem, the set 𝒟[a,b]\mathcal{D}_{[a,b]} is compact under τ𝒟\tau_{\mathcal{D}}. Since γ|𝒟[a,b]\gamma|_{\mathcal{D}_{[a,b]}} is τ𝒟\tau_{\mathcal{D}}-continuous (as γ\gamma is Lebesgue continuous), for all ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that

dBL​(Q,P)<δ⟹|γ⁡(Q)−γ⁡(P)|<ϵ,Q,P∈𝒟[a,b].d_{\mathrm{BL}}(Q,P)<\delta\implies|\gamma(Q)-\gamma(P)|<\epsilon,\penalty\ \penalty\ Q,P\in\mathcal{D}_{[a,b]}. (15)

Given ϵ>0\epsilon>0, find δ>0\delta>0 such that (15) holds. Now find N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} such that supν∈𝒫dBL​((Xn)#​ν,X#​ν)<δ\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}d_{\mathrm{BL}}((X_{n})_{\#}\nu,X_{\#}\nu)<\delta for all n≥Nn\geq N. For each n≥Nn\geq N, let μn∈𝒫\mu_{n}\in\mathcal{P} satisfy supν∈𝒫γ⁡(Xn|ν)=γ⁡(Xn|μn).\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}}\gamma(X_{n}|\nu)=\gamma(X_{n}|\mu_{n}).

Therefore,

ρ⁡(Xn)−ρ⁡(X)≤γ⁡(Xn|μn)−γ⁡(X|μn)<ϵ.\rho(X_{n})-\rho(X)\leq\gamma(X_{n}|\mu_{n})-\gamma(X|\mu_{n})<\epsilon.

Thus limn→∞ρ⁡(Xn)=ρ⁡(X)\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho(X_{n})=\rho(X), and ρ\rho is Lebesgue continuous. ∎

Verification 5.

For all X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, the mapping 𝔼ϵKL∘ιX\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{KL}}\circ\iota_{X} is Σ\Sigma-measurable.

Proof.

Since 𝔼ϵKL\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{KL}} is Lebesgue continuous, by Proposition 13, 𝔼ϵKL∘ιX\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{KL}}\circ\iota_{X} is Σ\Sigma-measurable for X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}. ∎

Proof of Proposition 11.

Given μ∈Δ\mu\in\Delta, by Ahmadi-Javid (2012, Theorem 3.3),

𝔼ϵKL​(X|μ)=infz>0z⁡(log⁡(𝔼μ​[eX/z])+ϵ),X∈𝒳b.\mathbb{E}^{\mathrm{KL}}_{\epsilon}(X|\mu)=\inf_{z>0}z\left(\log\left(\mathbb{E}^{\mu}\left[e^{X/z}\right]\right)+\epsilon\right),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b}.

Therefore, it is clear that, for all X∈𝒳bX\in\mathcal{X}_{b}, 𝔼ϵKL∘ιX\mathbb{E}^{\mathrm{KL}}_{\epsilon}\circ\iota_{X} is concave.

Let X∈𝒞bX\in\mathcal{C}_{b}. As 𝔼ϵKL\mathbb{E}^{\mathrm{KL}}_{\epsilon} is Lebesgue continuous, by Proposition 12, 𝔼ϵKL∘ιX\mathbb{E}^{\mathrm{KL}}_{\epsilon}\circ\iota_{X} is τ\tau-continuous. Therefore, −𝔼KLϵ∘ιX-\mathbb{E}^{\mathrm{KL}}_{\epsilon}\circ\iota_{X} is convex and τ\tau-continuous. Therefore, by the definition of ≥cx\geq_{\mathrm{cx}}, for all π~,π∈Π\tilde{\pi},\pi\in\Pi satisfying π~≥cxπ\tilde{\pi}\geq_{\mathrm{cx}}\pi, we have

∫Δ−𝔼ϵKL(X|ν)π~(dν)≥∫Δ−𝔼ϵKL(X|ν)π(dν).\int_{\Delta}-\mathbb{E}^{\mathrm{KL}}_{\epsilon}(X|\nu)\tilde{\pi}(\mathrm{d}\nu)\geq\int_{\Delta}-\mathbb{E}^{\mathrm{KL}}_{\epsilon}(X|\nu)\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu).

Since X∈𝒞bX\in\mathcal{C}_{b} was arbitrary, by Proposition 14, we have

∫Δ−𝔼ϵKL(X|ν)π~(dν)≥∫Δ−𝔼ϵKL(X|ν)π(dν),X∈𝒳b,\int_{\Delta}-\mathbb{E}^{\mathrm{KL}}_{\epsilon}(X|\nu)\tilde{\pi}(\mathrm{d}\nu)\geq\int_{\Delta}-\mathbb{E}^{\mathrm{KL}}_{\epsilon}(X|\nu)\pi(\mathrm{d}\nu),\penalty\ \penalty\ X\in\mathcal{X}_{b},

and the proof is complete. ∎
